body: It is the first Monday in two weeks without rain on it, and the Commons has put the patio tables back out like a town putting out flags, each one wiped down by somebody who didn’t want to be the one who hadn’t, the undersides still beaded. The sprinklers on the lawn have come back on, Marisol’s way of announcing that it believes the weather. Jack has the table nearest the glass doors, in the sun, with the Carhartt over the back of the chair and a plate of eggs he has had four peaceful bites of.
The RAZR goes off against the tabletop at 7:44, and goes off again, and then keeps going in a run, as it does for exactly one person at this hour.

body: He doesn’t answer the last one. He holds the phone open until the screen goes dark by itself, and his other hand goes back over the chair to the Carhartt and stays on the collar.

Kevin and Margot are across from him, Kevin with his oatmeal and a banana he is cutting into thirds with the edge of a spoon, Margot with her hot water and a legal pad she hasn’t opened. Neither has asked why he is holding the RAZR in his hand like something that might bite. It’s Monday. People are allowed to look at a phone.

Theo comes across the patio at ten of eight with the iPhone held out in front of him like a hymnal. The gold pin is on the lapel of the blazer; Hollis, retired with honors, is back in his teacup on the nightstand in 412. A brother since Saturday, Theo is insufferable before nine in a way he had to be taught, and he has evidently been up since six waiting for somebody to ask him why, and no one has. He sets the phone down by the butter, turns it a quarter turn toward Jack with one finger, and sits.

“Good morning, Costigan. Please remain seated.” He reads the headline in the voice that comes right before the weather. “‘Sweetwater’s Skye Callender marches with pro-lifers — and who’s her mystery guy?’” He looks up. “They don’t know. It’s the one honest sentence on the internet.”
He scrolls it for the table a photograph at a time.

body: Jack has been photographed at his Confirmation and for the Mooney yearbook, and never from behind, by strangers, with a caption. Under the item the comments begin, and Theo, unasked, reads three of them in three voices. “‘Mystery Guy looks like he’s about to apologize to a nun,’” in a woman’s alto. “‘That’s not a Catholic school boy, that’s a Teamster,’” in a baritone, from a user called UnionMaid4Life. And in a breathless soprano, from a user who has not read the item: “‘is he single.’”

The phone goes around. Kevin reads it with both thumbs and goes the color of his oatmeal. “There’s a thread,” he says. “About the jacket. Somebody’s linked the catalog.” He scrolls. “In fairness, it’s the right model.” He hands the phone on quickly. “My GPA was on the internet once. In high school. It was a typo — somebody transposed a nine — and it took a semester to come down, and in that semester a girl in my AP Chem lab stopped lending me her good pen. I want you to know I understand.”

Margot takes it last and reads it through to the end with her hot water going cold at her elbow, wearing the face she keeps for a field report. “The internet has identified you by your outerwear,” she says, and slides the phone back to Theo. “In my discipline that’s called material culture. You are a garment, Costigan. Congratulations. Do you own another coat? As a matter of method.”
“It’s January.”
“He has one coat,” Theo says. “It isn’t a wardrobe, it’s a vow.”
Kevin wants a statement drafted. “Short. Dignified. Nothing about the jacket.”
“No statements,” says Theo. “The first rule of Mystery Guy is that he doesn’t know he’s Mystery Guy.”

Doug Pruitt arrives with a tray of hash browns and his own phone already out, and stops at the end of the table as if somebody had hung a velvet rope there. “Dude,” he says, in all five vowels. “You’re *Mystery Guy*.”
“I’m aware.”

“A girl in the omelet line showed me. I said, *he’s got that jacket*, and she said, ‘That’s the whole point,’ and I still didn’t get it till I sat down.” He sits. “That’s so weird. You’re like a ghost that has a coat.”

“Kenzie’s very proud of the album,” Kevin says. He has put his spoon down for it. “She doesn’t know it’s public. I’m going to tell her. Gently. Today.” He takes a folded index card out of his shirt pocket and consults it. “I have notes.”
At 7:58 the RAZR lights on the table, and this one he picks up.

body: Doug asks if it’s Gina. “It’s Skye,” Jack says. “I’m required at a lunch.”
“Is that, like, an honor?”
“It’s an interview with bread.”

By the cereal bar a table of Louisiana kids who have been up since six for no reason but joy puts one of its members on a chair, and he calls it — *Who dat?* — and the Commons answers, even the omelet line, two weeks out from Miami. Jack keeps his eyes on the eggs. He doesn’t look toward the window tables.
Theo wipes the iPhone’s screen on his lapel and lays it face down. “As your roommate, your friend and a man with a pin,” he says, “what do we do about Mystery Guy?”

response: “Brass,” Theo says at once, and the hand with the pin goes up and cuts the air, already seeing it. “A serif. MYSTERY GUY, EST. 2010. I’ll have it by Friday.”
“Brass is a choice,” says Margot.

Doug wants to know whether it goes on the door of 412 or on the door of the Commons, and Theo says that is the kind of question that wins grants. Kevin, who has been waiting for someone to ask him to be reasonable, asks whether a plaque is the best response to a thread. “It is the only response,” says Theo, “that comes with a ceremony.”
The table goes quiet. Doug has a hash brown halfway to his mouth. “Who’s Danny?”
Theo, who sat across a table from Danny on Christmas Eve with a bag of vending-machine pretzels between them, doesn’t look at Jack. “His brother,” he says. “It’s a very good jacket.”
Kevin slides his tray across the table until it touches Jack’s, and eats his oatmeal. Doug lowers the hash brown.

Jack closes the RAZR and picks up his fork. Doug, who has never been refused a screen in his life, takes Theo’s iPhone off the table and reads the comments aloud instead, with feeling — a woman’s indignation, a man’s theory about the tan of the Carhartt — until Kevin lifts the phone out of his hand. “That’s enough of the public.”
“The public was just getting interesting,” says Margot, and goes back to her hot water, aggrieved on behalf of the field.

s02.slug: MONDAY · 11:50 AM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM
body: Tomás’s record comes up through the floorboards — something new and quick, a drum that won’t sit down and a guitar skating along the top of it — loud enough in the front room that up here it’s in the mattress. On the way in he stepped around Sol’s swing on the porch: the driftwood seat lying on the boards under its two hooks, a coil of new chain beside it, not hung yet. In her room the blind is up and the window over the mattress is open on a washed, bright noon, and the light comes in white off the water and lies across the sheets.

Skye is cross-legged in the middle of the mattress in his flannel from the Walk — she never gave it back, and he never asked — and not much else, with the white iPhone in her lap. She looks up at him in the doorway, and at the Carhartt over his arm, and she is already somebody else.
“*Corinne Waxman*,” she says.

It’s all of Corinne’s hello, the name and nothing after it, and she has the vowels exactly: pleasant, rounded, immovable, a voice that has heard every objection there is and finds all of them a little sad. She takes a sip out of a coffee cup that isn’t there. “Good morning. You’re on a website. Not one of the good ones — one of the ones that would *like* to be one of the good ones. There’s a march. There’s a boy. And there is a coat.” Her eyes go to the Carhartt. “The coat is a problem, Skye. The coat has a following.”
He drops it on the floor by the door. She nods at it, satisfied, in Corinne’s face.
“Does the coat get a lawyer?” he says.
“The coat gets *managed*.”
“What do I get?”
“You,” says Corinne, kindly, with real regret, “get lunch.”

Then the rules, in Corinne’s voice, off a BlackBerry made of nothing. Every picture of the two of them comes down: hers, and anybody’s she can reach, and anybody’s she can’t reach Corinne will reach. Nothing new goes up. Not a picture. Not a status. “Not a *mood*.” And all of it — she leans on every syllable of the word and drops a little curtsy at the end of it — “until we have a *strategy*.” Lunch tomorrow. Studio City. Her mother will be there. Something with sleeves.

He laughs. She’s very good. She reads him the comments in Corinne’s voice, as Corinne would read a ransom note into the minutes: one of them thinks he’s a Jonas Brother; one of them thinks he’s her bodyguard; one of them would very much like to know whether he is single, and has used a great many exclamation points to ask. She does a man from the network wanting to know, very gently, whether Cassidy is pro-life now, in Corinne doing the man from the network. She does the man from the network’s lawyer. She does her own mother finding out, in Corinne doing Debbie doing Corinne, and the voices go up on top of one another, each one starting before the last one has finished, and none of them stops anywhere. She’s going faster. The bit keeps finding more bit, and there’s nowhere at the bottom of it to land.
Somewhere around her mother he quits laughing. He sits down on the end of the mattress and watches her.
She’s in the middle of *strategy* again when she sees he’s stopped. The word comes apart in Corinne’s mouth halfway through, and there’s no one left in her voice to finish it.
She looks down at the phone in her lap. Downstairs the song runs out and the next one starts.
“I liked being the only thing in my life nobody wrote,” she says.
He hasn’t got anything for that that isn’t a joke, so he doesn’t give her one. He takes the phone out of her lap and sets it on the sheet behind her, out of the way.
She takes hold of the front of his shirt with both fists and pulls him down onto the mattress by it, and this time he doesn’t wait to be pulled the rest of the way.

He has had it in him since the porch. Since before the porch, if he’s honest — since a square of sun crossing her wall on Friday, since a fogged windshield at Pismo; it came up Del Playa with him and in at her door and up her stairs two at a time. He rolls her under him onto the sheet and kisses her as if he has quit arguing with himself, and she laughs into it, surprised, and then she isn’t laughing. He has never been the one to start this. It turns out he knows how. The flannel is soft as a dish towel from a hundred washes on Glenwood Avenue, and he is the one who goes for the buttons. The top one, and his mouth on the collarbone it gives him. The second, and the hollow of her throat, and the place between her breasts where her skin is warm from the sheet. Her back comes up off the mattress into his hands. He works the third button through with his knuckles against her and the flannel falls open on her left side into the white noon from the window, and he takes her breast in his mouth, and she makes a sound that isn’t any word and holds his head there with both hands in his hair. Her bare knee slides up along his ribs and hooks there. She gets a hand down between them and opens his belt by feel, the tongue pulled out of the keeper and the buckle falling loose against his stomach, and the heel of her hand comes down hard on the front of his jeans, and he pushes up into it before he knows he has, and she breathes something into his hair he has never heard her say for any camera. Under his mouth her heart is going hard and fast. His hand goes to the fourth button.
Her hand comes down flat over his.

Not pushing. Holding. Her other hand has gone still on his open belt, exactly where it was, and it stays there; she doesn’t take it away and she doesn’t move it, and that is worse than either. She keeps her palm over the back of his hand and his hand over her heart, and he lifts his head. Her mouth is red where he had it, and her hair is all over the sheet, and her eyes are open on his, steady, already decided.
“Sunday,” she says.
It takes him a second to find it. Downstairs the record goes on without either of them.

“I sat next to you,” Skye says. “Two hundred people in their good shoes went up past you, and the lady with the beads, and you knelt there with your hands like this —” she takes his hand off her and laces her fingers through it between them, to show him “— and I sat there knowing every one of them could see why.” Her thumb moves on his knuckle. “I said once is a scandal. On the porch. I wasn’t doing a bit.”
“I’m going Wednesday,” he says.
“I know you are.”

“So —” He can hear where the sentence goes before he gets there, and he goes there anyway, with his mouth an inch from hers and the rest of him not listening to either of them. “So it’s going in on Wednesday anyway.”
She looks at him a long moment from the sheet: the look from the Embarcadero, the one that finds the soft place in an argument and puts a thumb on it.

“I read about it,” she says. “Sunday night, after the porch. The whole section, with a highlighter, like sides the night before a table read. You have to be sorry. You have to mean you won’t do it again. There’s a word for it.”
“Amendment.”
“*Purpose* of amendment.” She has it exactly; she probably has the page number. “You can’t walk in there Wednesday with a plan, Jack. I read that part three times. I’m not going to be your plan.”

“You told me Friday it was turning into not yet,” she says. “In the sun. You said *probably*.” Her hand is still on his belt, still not moving. “Fine. You don’t get to be the one who says not yet. I’m saying it. Not this week. Not *never* — I don’t say never, I’m in the business, never is how they get you to sign things. Not this week. Ask me again after you go up.”
“After Sunday.”
“After I *watch* you go up. I want to be sitting there when you do. Once. And know I didn’t cost you it.”
She takes her hand off his belt then, and he feels where it was all the way down.
And then she doesn’t let go of him. He did not expect that either.

She rolls him — he lets her — and comes up astride him in the flannel, open to the third button and not one button further, and takes both his wrists and puts them down on the sheet over his head, and holds them there with one hand. Her thumb tests his grip, once. When he doesn’t pull, she smiles. “Hold still,” she says. “That’s all. You hold still, and I hold still, and nobody goes anywhere.”

They don’t. She sits on him with her whole weight settled where his belt hangs open, the long bare backs of her thighs along his hips, and doesn’t move, and he can feel the heat of her through the denim and every breath she takes in it, and she can feel exactly what that is doing to him, because there is nothing between them but his jeans and a little cotton and she is sitting on it. His hips come up off the sheet once, by themselves. She puts him back down with her knees and goes on not moving. Her thighs are trembling against him with the work of it. He can feel that too.

She bends down until her hair closes the noon off around both their faces, and puts her mouth at his ear, and in her own voice, the one with no character in it, she tells him what Sunday buys. She’s specific. She takes her time. The blind up, she says, like Friday. The flannel off, all of it, and her on her back in the square of sun this time, and his mouth where it went on Friday, slower, because now they both know what she sounds like when she isn’t doing a voice, and she wants him to hear it from the start; and then hers, on him, and her eyes up on his the whole time. He couldn’t stand that on Friday, and couldn’t stop looking. She names each thing in its order, plainly, like a call sheet read back over a phone, and every one of them goes through him like current, and she still hasn’t moved. His wrists are pulling against her hand without his permission. He says her name like a complaint. She gets as far as *and then* —
She lifts her head off his ear an inch.
“Does this count?” she says. “The talking.”
He could lie to her. She would hear it before he had finished. He is flat on his back with his wrists over his head and his belt open, and he would hear it too.
“Yes.”

She looks at him from very close. Whatever crosses her face is aimed at herself, and isn’t only amusement. “Of course it does,” she says. “It’s the good part.” She doesn’t get off him. She straightens up, still astride, and lets go of his wrists one finger at a time, and sets both her hands on her own knees where he can see them. “Okay. Then that’s where it is. Nothing that’s going anywhere. I get to sit here. I’m not the one saying it to him on Wednesday.”

He doesn’t argue. It might be the first no she has ever had a reason for that wasn’t only hers; he can see her finding out what she can build on one, and he lies under it and lets her build. Over her shoulder the clock on the dresser says 12:21. Hale is at one.

She reaches out across the sheet without looking, finds the phone by feel, and holds it up at the end of her arm above the two of them, the back of it to the ceiling and the little lens turned down on them, blind. She can’t see what it sees. That seems to be the idea.
“Don’t move,” she says, against his jaw, as if he had. And then, very low, right into his ear, in Corinne’s vowels: “*A friend from school.*”
He laughs with his eyes shut — he can’t help it — and above them the phone makes its little fake shutter noise.

She brings it down and looks at it by herself. All he can see is the white back of it and her face over it, lit from underneath. She gives one short breath through her nose at whatever’s there. She reaches over the edge of the mattress and lays it face down on the floorboards, on the far side of her, and puts her hands back on her knees.
“What do you call me?” she says. “In there. To him.”
“I don’t say your name.”
“I know you don’t say my name. What do you call it?”
He could find her a softer word. There are softer words. He looks up at her with the noon on her and gives her the real one, because she would hear the other.
“The near occasion of sin.”

He was raised on that phrase. It was on a poster over the pencil sharpener in second grade at St. Brigid’s; Nonna has it in Italian; he has said it at the end of every Act of Contrition since he was seven, *and to avoid the near occasion of sin*, at the speed you say a thing you’ve said a thousand times. He has never heard it said back to him from on top of him, with his own shirt open on her, after going and learning it on a Sunday night for his sake.

She tries it slowly, a line somebody has handed her cold. “The near occasion.” Something goes across her face that is a laugh and isn’t one. “That’s the best billing I’ve ever had.” And then, plainly: “I don’t want to be the occasion, Jack. I want to be the —”
She stops. Whatever it was, she had it all the way to her teeth, and he watches her put it back.
“The what?”
“Never mind. It’s not ready.” She looks at the window instead of at him. “Tell me what I’m saving you. Sunday. If you sit in the pew. Not the book — you.”

So he tries, on his back, in words that aren’t anybody’s. That it isn’t the rule. That he was seven, in a white suit at St. Brigid’s and Danny’s old dress shoes with Kleenex in the toes, and every week since then it has been the one thing he doesn’t have to be good at: you go up and open your hands and it’s put in them, the same as Nonna’s, the same as the guy behind you with the neck tattoo, and nobody asks what you got on the test. And when he can’t go, he sits there and watches it go up the aisle past him, row by row, to everybody he came in with. “It’s like Sunday dinner,” he says, “and they pass the plate around you. Nobody says anything. They just pass it over you.”
She has listened to all of it with her hands on her knees.

“I watched them pass it over you,” she says. “I didn’t know that’s what I was watching.” She’s quiet a moment. Downstairs the song changes. “The book says you stay away from it. The near occasion. I read that part too.” She looks down at him, and her voice doesn’t do anything at all. “So if he tells you on Wednesday to stay away from me — would you?”

You said no, and told her he’d never say it: what’s good between you isn’t something to avoid, and the bad doesn’t cancel it out. She asked if Friday counted as good; you told her Friday was in both columns.
response: It doesn’t land as he meant it. She flinches.

“Don’t,” she says. She is off him for the first time since the fourth button, back on her heels on the sheet with the flannel pulled closed in one fist. “Don’t hand me that like a present. That’s the sentence they’d put under the picture. *She got him to choose.*” Her knuckles have gone white on the flannel. “If he says it, you go home and you think about it. And I’ll be the one who keeps your Sunday, because somebody in this room has to have read the book.”
He doesn’t take it back. He sits up, so they’re level on the sheet, his belt still hanging open and her knees a foot from his.
“He wouldn’t, though,” he says. “That’s what I’m telling you. He wouldn’t say it.”
“You don’t know that.”

“I do. I went in there last fall sure that’s what I was going to get. I had my bag packed for it.” He can see the closet, the screen, the Prodigal Son tacked up at the height of a kneeling man’s eyes. “He asked me one question. Did I want to stop seeing you, or stop what happens. And then he told me to change the hour. Keep you in the daylight.” He looks at the window, at the white noon coming in off the water, and back at her. “That’s what he’d say Wednesday. Same thing. He’s not going to tell me to quit you. He’s going to tell me to quit *this*, and put my shirt on, and take you to lunch.”
Her fist hasn’t moved on the flannel. But she’s listening the way she listens to a director, for the note under the note.

“He says there’s a lot of good between two people,” Jack says. “Between us. And what’s good isn’t something you have to stay away from. You don’t avoid it. You’re not supposed to.” He has to go slower for the next part, because it’s the part he believes. “It doesn’t make up for the bad. I’m not saying that. I’m not walking in there Wednesday with you as my excuse. But it goes both ways, Skye. The bad doesn’t cancel out the good, either. It doesn’t get to.”
Downstairs the record has run out, and Tomás hasn’t turned it over, and for a moment there’s no sound in the house but the sea doing what it does under the window.
“Say the last part again.”
“The bad doesn’t cancel out the good.”

She looks at him a long time from the end of the mattress. He watches it reach her, and he watches her decide not to make a bit out of it, which costs her something; he can see the bit go by, fully built, and her let it.
“That’s not in the book,” she says.
“It’s in him.”
“Which him?” Her eyes narrow at him over her knuckles. “You, or the priest? I’ve worked with a lot of men who say *the director wants* when what they mean is *I want*, and they all had your face on.”

“The daylight’s his. Last fall, word for word.” He doesn’t hurry the rest; she would hear him hurry it. “The last part’s mine. I think it’s his too. I’ll find out Wednesday. I’m going to have to tell him I put words in his mouth on your bed.”

“Good. Tell him they were good words.” She keeps her fist where it is. She puts up her other hand instead, palm out, a script supervisor stopping a take. “Okay. Columns. Who keeps them? Who decides which one I go in?”
“You don’t go in one.” He is sure of this; it’s the oldest thing he knows. “The columns are for what I did. You’re not something I did.”
She stares at him. “That’s a very Catholic way to tell a girl she isn’t a mistake.”
“It’s the only way I know how to say anything.”
“Then say the bad.” The hand comes down. “Not the book word. Not *occasion*. In English, in this room. I’ll know if you sand it.”

So he says it in English, with his eyes on hers. Friday afternoon, with the blind up. Saturday night at Pismo, until a gearshift got there first. Twenty minutes ago, his hand on the fourth button, and him not the one who stopped. It never takes long, in English.
She hears it out without blinking. Her knuckles on the flannel have gone from white to pink. “And the good,” she says. “Friday. Does Friday go in the good too? Or do I just get lunch?”

“Both,” he says. “Friday’s in both.” He makes himself go slow again. “You in that square of sun on your wall. That you trusted me with it. That I wanted you so bad I couldn’t see straight — I’m not confessing that, Skye. God made that part. I’m confessing what I did with it. It’s the same afternoon. It all goes in on Wednesday, and none of it cancels.”
“That’s a terrible system.”
“It’s two thousand years old,” he says. “It’s the only one that ever worked on me.”
The light has come across the sheet while they talked and lies over her bare knees now, white off the water. She looks at it there before she says anything.

“You know what the good part of a shot is? A bounce card under your chin and a kicker in your hair, and a man named Lou up a ladder with a flag. For forty seconds you’re the good thing in the episode. Then they strike the lights, and you’re a girl who costs money.” Her thumb goes along the seam of the flannel. “I’ve been the good thing in a lot of scenes, Jack. I’ve never been it with the lights off.”
“They’re off.”
“You call that off?” She tips her chin at the window. “It’s noon.”
“That’s the priest’s,” he says. “Daylight. It doesn’t count as lighting.”

Her mouth goes unsteady, and she shuts it, and presses the back of her wrist hard against her nose until whatever was coming has been talked out of it. When she takes the wrist down her eyes are wet, and she looks furious with them.
“The thing I put back,” she says. “Before. It came up again just now.”
“And?”
“And it’s closer. And it still isn’t ready. Right now it would come out sounding like *thank you*. I don’t pay for this. You don’t get paid.”
She points a finger at him. “And none of it moves Sunday. Don’t make that face. You were going to try.”
“A little.”

“A little is how they get you to sign things.” But she has run out of fight to put in it, and she lowers it. “Okay.” Her fingers come open on the flannel one at a time, and it falls loose again where she had it closed. She doesn’t fix it. “Then it’s not a present. It’s a — ” and there is Corinne, for half a second, with the vowels rounded and the eyebrows up: “— *strategy*.” And gone again, and just Skye, quieter than he has ever heard her in this room. “I can live in the daylight column, Jack. I’ve been lit worse.”

At a quarter to one she walks him to her door in the flannel, done back up to the throat, and nothing on her feet, and reaches up and straightens his collar, carefully, with both hands, with no camera anywhere at the bottom of the stairs. “There,” she says. “Now you look like somebody’s friend from school.” She shuts the door on him. He’s on the second step down when she opens it again, to look, and shuts it again.

At a quarter to one she’s on her stomach with her chin on her crossed arms, watching him hunt the floor for his shoes, and she doesn’t help. One of them is under the dresser. She knew. He gets it on standing up, hopping, buckling his belt with the other hand, and goes down the stairs past Tomás’s door with the record still going, out across the porch around the swing seat, and up Del Playa toward campus with his laces untied.

s03.slug: MONDAY · 1:02 PM · HOLLIS HALL, 302 — THE CONVERSION OF ST. PAUL
body: He takes the Hollis stairs fast and comes into 302 at two minutes past one, still ahead of Hale, with his pulse somewhere back down Del Playa and his face warm to the ears. He sits at the door end under the clock and puts both hands around a pen, because they want something to hold.

It’s Monday’s room. Evan is at the door with the roster on its clipboard, ticking names with a click of the pen. Yusuf has the corner and a coffee. The two girls from the window side are comparing their *Frankenstein*s, whose spines broke at the same chapter. At the window end, in the last chair, Lena has *The End of the Affair* out already for Thursday, set true to the edge of the table, with her *Frankenstein* under it, finished, and the pencil laid across the pair.

Caleb has his phone under the lip of the table again, tilted toward Yusuf, and says it at the volume of a man who believes he is whispering. “Costigan’s on a celebrity blog. Not Perez. One of the ones that wants to be Perez.”
Yusuf looks at the phone, and at Jack. “Congratulations?”
At the window end, Lena turns a page.

Hale comes in at six minutes past with wine on his cuff and his coat over his arm, takes the roster from Evan without reading it, and sees the phone. He sits down halfway along the side, where he has to turn his head for either end, and looks delighted with the calendar.

“Today,” he tells the table, “is the Conversion of St. Paul. I looked it up, so that you wouldn’t have to. It is the only conversion story I have ever found credible. A man falls off a horse and is never the same again.” He lifts a finger. “There is no horse in Acts, incidentally. Caravaggio supplied the horse. The Church has always been generous with livestock.”
He turns his head down the table to Caleb, unhurried, and says it the way it ought to be said, each word set down where it goes:
“*Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?*”
“Dude,” says Caleb, and the phone goes into his bag.

They finish *Frankenstein*. Hale does the ending himself, because none of them, he says, can be trusted with it. “Victor dies apologizing to a sea captain, which is the most English thing a Swiss has ever done. The creature gets the last speech, and the best one, and then Mrs. Shelley puts him on a raft of ice and sends him off to burn himself somewhere none of us can check. *Lost in darkness and distance.* She was nineteen, and she knew where to stop.” He looks around the table. “Several of you are nineteen.”
“He said he’d do it,” Yusuf says. “He kept every other promise in the book.”
“Noorzai has read the book,” says Hale. “Make a note, Mr. Marsh. It may not happen again.”

With ten minutes left he folds his hands on the roster. “Thursday I shall be in New York, being rude to a churchman on a stage, for money. Greene therefore moves. Wednesday, six o’clock, at my house. Some of you know the way.” At the window end the pencil stops. “The President is addressing the nation at the same hour. I intend to have him on, and we shall treat him as the warm-up act. Bring a guest. The speech is long and the wine is cheap.” Evan writes it on the clipboard. “Phones go in the dog’s bowl at the door. House rule. Berkeley is deaf, and I should like the rest of you to try it.”

He turns his head to the door end, and then the long way round to the window end, so the table can watch him do it. “Mr. Costigan will defend Sarah Miles’s silence. Miss Broussard will prosecute it. You both spent last week arguing against yourselves on paper. I should like you back in your own clothes.”
Jack keeps his eyes on Hale.

“Fine,” Lena says — to Hale. She takes the pencil off the Greene and writes something small in the top margin of the first page, the address, probably, though she has been to that house before; and she lays the pencil back across the book where it was.

s04.slug: MONDAY · 7:45 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE 4TH-FLOOR LOUNGE
body: On the lounge television, sound off, a man in a suit points a marker at a map of Florida, and under him the crawl says SAINTS · COLTS · TWO WEEKS TO MIAMI. On the screen a quarterback in a black-and-gold helmet throws a football at the sky in slow motion, over and over, and the sky declines to catch it. It has been on since dinner, for company.

It is a Monday-night lounge. Doug is cross-legged on the carpet with a mug of cereal; Kevin has the middle couch to himself and a BlackBerry he keeps turning over; Margot has the armchair, a legal pad on the arm and her Docs flat on the floor; Theo, in the blazer, takes the other couch lengthwise with one shoe on the cushion. Jack has the Greene open on his knee, the Penguin with the cracked spine, to a page where it is raining on a London common. He is still on the page he started on. It is a good page.

Priya goes past the open door with a roll of tape and a fresh laminate, THE ELEVATOR IS NOT A WAITING ROOM. THIS MEANS YOU, and stops in the frame to say, to the lounge at large, “It’s for the elevator,” in case anyone had taken it for the lounge. She goes on to the elevator.

Kevin has been waiting all evening to report, and when Doug asks what is wrong with his face, he reports: the oldest Dominguez brother, Javi, has invited him to a 49ers game. A home game. With the family.
“Dude,” Doug says. “It’s January. The season’s over.”
“September,” says Kevin. “I have time to prepare. I looked up the stadium. I looked up the *parking*.”

Jack was in the lot at St. Brendan’s at midnight on Saturday when the van came home, under the sodium light, and saw the handshake at the side door. “How long was the handshake, Kev?” Kevin looks at him. “It was a normal handshake.” “How long,” says Doug. Kevin consults the ceiling. “It was a long normal handshake,” he says, and goes red to the ears, and is furious about going red.

Margot has been writing since the Embarcadero. The piece is for the Newman beat, about the women on the route with the signs, and she has a first sentence she will not read to anyone. “It contains the word *nuns*,” she tells Doug, for the fourth time, “and no adjective. I had to work for that. I won’t be workshopping it with a lounge.”
“The ones in the running shoes,” Jack offers.

“The shoes are in the second sentence. I will thank you not to compose my first.” She uncaps the pen. “On Wednesday the President addresses the nation. Does anyone propose to watch it, or are we all going to read about it in the *Times*, in the voice of a person who was in the room?”
“Is it a big deal?” Doug asks. “Or is it like the Oscars?”
“It’s the Oscars, Pruitt,” says Theo, “where one party stands up and the other sits on its hands, and then they switch for the next paragraph.”
“I would like to see whether he mentions Thursday’s decision,” Margot says. “The Court sits ten feet from the podium, in its robes, obliged by decorum to look at its lap.”
“He’s allowed,” Jack says. “It’s a speech.”
“Is it? Or is it an ambush with applause lines?”

“To answer your question,” Jack says, “Hale’s. He moved Greene up from Thursday. Wednesday at six, his house, the speech on his television. Bring a guest. The wine’s cheap, and phones go in the dog’s bowl.”
“The dog’s bowl,” says Doug, reverent.
“Costigan’s plus-one,” Theo announces, “has been selected.”
“I haven’t asked anyone.”

“That’s what makes it a selection.” He swings his shoe to the floor. “I shall bring a bottle. A ninety-four Rioja Reserva out of my grandfather’s cellar in Pasadena, given to him in ’96 by a Spanish ambassador who wept at the bouquet and was reassigned within the quarter. It has a story. It’s in the original crate.”
“You’re nineteen,” Kevin says.
“I am not drinking it, Tran. I am transporting it. The professor says the wine is cheap; I take that as an invitation.”
“And the girlfriend?” Margot says, to the legal pad.
“I hadn’t —”
“Out of the question,” says Theo. “Skye Callender at that table is a second feature. Hale would stop the seminar to ask her for notes.”
“He’d cite her,” Kevin says.
“He’d *hire* her.”
“Can *I* come?” says Doug.
“No, Pruitt.”
“Before that,” Jack says, because it will come out anyway, “I’ve got a lunch tomorrow. Studio City. Her mother and her publicist.”
“The Callender interview,” Theo says at once, and the lacquer is gone from his voice. “Don’t eat the bread.”
“What?”

“Debbie Callender once took a bread basket away from a grown man at a wrap party. I was twelve. I watched it from under a table.” He sits up. “She’ll ask after me. I’m Teddy to her; it’s the one thing she and my father agree on. Tell her I’m well, thriving, and in a fraternity.”
“Why would I tell her you’re in a fraternity?”
“Because she’ll be thrilled,” Theo says, “and it will buy you four minutes.”
In the corridor Laney goes past the lounge door at a walk, the pink BlackBerry held up before her, lit, and keeps going toward the stairs. Jack turns the page.
“She didn’t even look in,” Doug says.
“Observe the omission, Douglas,” says Margot. “It takes more effort than looking.”

Theo has watched Laney go without turning his head. When he speaks again it is idly, with his eyes on the muted quarterback. “Picture it, Costigan. Hypothetically. February the seventh. The Saints, in the Super Bowl. A man who no longer attends Sully’s.” The shoe goes back up on the cushion. “Where does that man watch it?”

response: “A radio,” Theo says. “In 2010.” His thumbs go to the iPhone. “Noted. For the hypothetical.”
“Which side?” says Margot.
“Ours.”
Theo types something and won’t say what.
Theo nods, too slowly, and types. Kevin watches him type. Kevin says nothing. It costs him.

s05.slug: MONDAY · 8:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL
body: The RAZR goes while he is still in the lounge with the Greene open on his knee, GINA across the little outside screen, and he is through the door and into the east stairwell with it against his ear before the third ring. His sister doesn’t call at this hour to say hello.

The landing is the one place in Delgado where the signal holds. He shoves the window up its six inches on a night that has finally stopped dripping, wet cement and eucalyptus and a sprinkler going somewhere below, and sits down on the top step.
“Are you alone?” Gina says.
She is whispering. Behind her something roars, level and endless: the fan in the upstairs bathroom on Glenwood Avenue, the only room in that house with a lock on the door.
“I’m in a stairwell.”
“Is that alone?”
“It’s Delgado. Gina. What.”

“Okay. Don’t freak out. It’s handled.” She takes a breath and goes fast, in order, with the footnotes in, as she has told him everything since she could talk. “It’s twenty of twelve here and I’m in the bathroom, so listen. You didn’t text back this morning. Which, fine. So after school I read all the comments, in the basement on the Dell, with Ma and Rosie still at St. Brigid’s and Nonna upstairs in her chair and Dad out in the garage with the radio. There’s like forty. And most of it’s the jacket. There’s a lady who thinks you’re a Teamster and wants to know if you’re single, and about nine people who think you’re a priest.”
“Gina —”
“And then number thirty-one.”
The fan covers whatever her voice does.

“He’s from home. His name has *Y-town* in it, and a three-three-oh. He said he knew whose jacket that was, and then he said convict.” Her voice goes up, and she pulls it down. “And then he said what for. The actual word. Like it was a fun fact.”

Jack’s free hand has found the stair rail, gray steel under years of gray paint, and he looks at it. There is a night he doesn’t think about. He is good at it, and he gets good at it again now, on purpose, with the sprinkler going below him and the dark standing in the window.

“I reported him,” Gina says. “There’s a button. It has a dropdown, spam or offensive or other. I picked other and typed *he’s wrong*, and then I went back and picked offensive too, just in case. But the button takes a day, so I answered him, too. I signed it. *His sister.* So he’d know who he said it in front of.”
“What did you say?”
“I called him a name.” The fan. “A Catholic one. So it doesn’t count.”
“I’m pretty sure it counts.”

“It doesn’t count *count*.” She hurries on, over it. “They took it down at nine. I checked at nine and ten and eleven and then ten after, in case. It’s just the jacket again. None of them even knew it was Danny’s. They were so *sure* about you. You were a Teamster.” Her breath catches on the next part and she runs straight through the catch. “People say stuff, Jack. I know what to do when people say stuff. You say it right back, and you don’t cry till the door’s locked.”
“Gina.”
“It’s the fan. It dries out your eyes.”

The Carhartt is on its hook in 412, where he left it, and he is cold in a way the window doesn’t account for. He wants to be on Glenwood Avenue, in the upstairs hall, on the floor with his back against that door, as he sat against it the night she was nine and the Browns lost in the last minute. He is a continent from the hall. He has a stair rail and a paperback, and a sister who has just gone brisk.
“You shouldn’t have had to read them,” he says.
“You weren’t going to.”
“I was.”
“You were going to read the first six and make a joke.”
He has one ready. It is a good one, and he puts it away.
“Don’t tell Ma,” Gina says. “She’ll want to know why I was on the Dell, and then she’ll ask Dad something, and then —” She doesn’t finish the then.
“She finds out everything, Gina. Eventually.”
“Not this week.”
“Where is she now?”

“Downstairs doing Rosie’s lunch for tomorrow. She makes it at night so the bread doesn’t go wet.” Under the fan, very faint, a cupboard door shuts, and another: a sound he could pick out of a thousand. “She thinks I’m on the toilet. I’m on the toilet. Technically.”
It is nearly midnight where she is.
“And Danny, either. He’d want the guy’s name, and what’s he supposed to do with a name in there.”
“I won’t.”

“Okay.” The roar changes pitch; she has switched the phone to the other ear. “Other thing. It’s the second, a week from tomorrow. Candlemas. Danny’s twenty-three.” Jack knows the room he will be twenty-three in, down to the smell of it. “Are you sending him something? Because I’m making him a card, and it has a candle on it, obviously, it’s *Candlemas*, and I need to know if yours is going to be better so I can stop.”
“Mine’s going to be a card.”
“Put it in my envelope. It’s one stamp.”
“You don’t have to —”
“It’s a stamp, Jack.” Beside her the toilet flushes, for cover. “I have to go. Ma’s going to think I have a condition.”
“Gina —”

On her end there is only the fan. Then, in the voice she used at nine, coming in from the yard with a skinned knee and not saying it hurt: “ok.” Small. “night jack.”

Jack knew there was a picture. At noon she looked at it, and laughed once, and laid the phone face down on her floorboards, and he didn’t ask. He did not know it was going anywhere. No one has ever shown him himself from above. The boy in it looks happy, and a little stupid with it, and Jack doesn’t mind either one. Under the picture the caption says *my friend from school*. And the voice goes back on, up into the nose and over the Alleghenies. “And now. Youngstown. For Tommy Hritz, of St. Christine’s.”

s07.slug: TUESDAY · 10:20 AM · US-101 SOUTH, THE RINCON — THE SAAB
body: The Rincon is gray from end to end this morning: gray water, gray boulders stacked along the shoulder, a low gray lid of cloud that quits somewhere short of the islands, and out in the Channel the oil platforms standing on their legs in all of it. The top is up. Along the point the surfers sit their boards in black wetsuits, twenty or thirty of them strung out on the line, waiting on a swell that comes in long and slow out of the gray and doesn’t hurry for anybody.
Back up the coast, Dr. Fenner will take roll in Oceanography 1 at eleven and find all of Pair 41 gone. Jack’s RAZR is in his jacket with the whole morning in it. He leaves it there.

Her iPod is on: Spoon, the new record, a piano somebody is hitting with real conviction and a man singing over it like he hasn’t slept. Skye is driving in a dress her mother picked — lilac, sleeves to the wrist, a color he would bet the Saab she has never bought for herself — and her hair is up, smooth, every piece of it where it’s been told to be. Her sunglasses are pushed up into it. On the hook behind his seat hangs a garment bag with a second dress in it, in case the first one turns out to be wrong.

She’s been putting something on since Montecito, a mile at a time. At Summerland her voice still had its corners. Through Carpinteria she said *fine* about the weather, and about the lunch, and about her mother, and each time it came out a little rounder. By the Rincon it’s nearly finished: easy, warm, pleasant to the middle, a voice you could serve on a plate.
He lets her. He doesn’t say anything about the voice. He talks about the surfers instead — which ones are going to go and which ones are only out there sitting.
“Him,” he says. “Yellow board. He’s going.”
The yellow board turns and paddles and drops in late and makes it, and runs down the face toward the boulders with his arms out.
“Her. Not her. That guy’s never going.” Jack points with his chin. “That guy’s out there because his wife’s home.”
“That’s very Youngstown of you,” Skye says, in the new smooth voice, and watches the yellow board till it’s gone behind the riprap.
He asks her what her mother orders at lunch, because he’d like to know what he’s walking into.
“Oh, she’ll be fine,” Skye says. “Salad. Dressing on the side. It’ll be fine.” She says it twice, and the second one is smoother than the first, and she passes a produce truck on it.
At the county line she turns Spoon down to almost nothing and tells him about the post. He hasn’t asked.

“Corinne emailed at nine-forty last night,” she says. “She already said it on the phone at six in the morning, but Corinne likes things in an email. Subject line, *Going forward*. She cc’d my mother. Everything down. Every picture of us, mine and anybody’s. Until we have a strategy.” She checks the mirror, and changes lanes for nobody. “So I put one up.”
He’s seen it. So has his wall.
“Her own rule,” Skye says. “If anybody asks, you’re a friend from school.” The sunglasses are still up. Her eyes stay on the road. “So I put it in writing.”
A motorhome lumbers past them on the left with a bike on the back, and she waits for it to be gone.
“It wasn’t at you,” she says. “It was at them. And I didn’t ask you first.” She doesn’t dress that up. “I’m not going to say I’m sorry about that part. You’d hear me not mean it.”
They go by La Conchita, its little houses tucked up under a raw brown hill on the landward side, and the road keeps to the water. She turns Spoon off altogether.
“One rule for today,” she says. “Whatever my mother says about you — you don’t answer it. I answer it.”
“And if it gets bad,” she says, “bring her a coffee. It worked on a man with a megaphone.”
She looks over at him then, for the first time since the county line, and leaves the music off. She hasn’t asked him what he thinks of the post.

response: She laughs. It gets out past the voice before she can sand it down, up through the lilac, and he sees it surprise her.

And then she looks at him sideways for a mile anyway, checking him like a mirror before a lane change. There’s nothing on his face to find but what he said. “Say it like that at lunch,” she tells him finally, “and my mother will want to adopt you.” Ahead of them Ventura comes up out of the gray, the pier going out on its pilings and the brown hills standing behind the town.

choices.text: “Corinne’s going to have a stroke. I don’t care.”
response: “Everybody says they don’t care,” she says, and smiles at the road.
The sunglasses come back down. She drives on behind the dark lenses. “Say that to Corinne.”
“I will.”

She doesn’t answer that. He can see himself in the lenses, small and doubled, a man in his one blazer saying a true thing she hasn’t got anywhere to put yet. He doesn’t say it again. People who say it twice are selling it, and she grew up on a lot full of people selling it.
The Rincon runs out behind them. Ahead the road runs on along the water toward Ventura, and the last of the surfers are only black specks on the gray, sitting.
“It’s a very good picture,” she agrees, in the smooth voice, as if they were discussing somebody else’s. “You’re in it.”
“That’s what’s good about it.”
“Supporting,” she says. “Don’t get ideas about billing.”

At the next straightaway she checks his face — quick, sideways, the sunglasses still up — as if the answer might have changed since the last mile. It hasn’t. At the one after that she checks again. He keeps his eyes on the water so she can look as often as she needs to, and out past Pitas Point another line of surfers sits in the gray, waiting, going nowhere.

s08.slug: TUESDAY · 12:30 PM · VENTURA BOULEVARD, STUDIO CITY — A TABLE FOR FOUR
body: Ventura Boulevard at lunchtime is all glare. The sun comes straight down on the bank signs and the nail salons and the little valet podiums, on a man in a headset walking a very small dog, and the restaurant sits back from the sidewalk under a green awning with its name on it in script. Inside it’s cool and brown and loud in a low way, a long room of booths full of men in good shirts saying numbers into phones.

Skye gave him the lay of it in the lot while the valet held her door with his eyes on her. Her mother will have a legal pad, because her mother always has a legal pad. Corinne will have one too, today. Corinne only uses paper when a lawyer might read it later.

There are two on the cloth when they get to the back. Debbie Callender is already up. She’s out of the booth before they reach it, in camel today, gold at her ears, and her hand is on Jack’s sleeve before he’s got hello out, and she’s already talking. “*Teddy*,” she says. “Tell me. Is Teddy eating? Is that father of his still impossible?”
“Both,” Jack says. “He’s in a fraternity.”
“Oh, *good*,” says Debbie, without saying to which, and steers him by the elbow into the inside of the booth, next to Skye, across from the pads.

Corinne Waxman doesn’t get up. She’s in black, with the one gold clip, and her BlackBerry lies face up by her bread plate like a fifth place setting. “Corinne,” she says — all of hello — and shakes his hand without taking her other thumb off the scroll wheel. The top sheet of her pad is already full, small upright writing in black ink, with printed pages clipped underneath. She folds the sheet over before he can read it upside down.
“Hi, Mother,” Skye says. “Corinne, hi.” She says it in the voice she finished on the Rincon, and sits, and spreads her napkin in her lap, and smiles at everybody.

Two booths down, a girl with a shopping bag has her phone up — a pink flip, held sideways, not quite pointed at them — and Skye’s smile is on and turned toward it before she has turned her head. It stays on until the phone goes down. It comes back to the table, the same smile, for her mother.

Debbie orders for the table without opening a menu: chopped salads, dressing on the side, and then she looks at Jack for a moment, measuring. “He’ll have the chicken,” she tells the waiter. “Boys like the chicken.” He does like the chicken.
“He wore the blazer,” she tells Corinne. “Corinne. He wore the *blazer* again.”
“I saw,” says Corinne.
“And it’s still philosophy?” Debbie says.
“Still philosophy.”
Corinne doesn’t look up. “Still not employable,” she says.
It’s the only jacket he owns that isn’t a Carhartt. The Carhartt is in the Saab’s trunk, where Skye put it this morning in the Delgado lot, folded, without a word about it.
Corinne runs the agenda off the pad, item by item, like a menu she’s sick of, and after each one lands Debbie leans in with her pen and softens it.

“One,” Corinne says. “The item.” She has it printed in color, the pink-and-black banner across the top of the page. “Two weeks ago I said we could live with the blogs. A blurry girl and the back of a coat is a rumor, and rumors are free.” She turns the page face down. “This one isn’t free. This one has a march in it.”
She looks up at Jack for the first time. “They’ve found your coat. They haven’t printed your name. They will — your name I can’t do anything about.” A small mark. “The coat I’d retire.”
“No,” Jack says.
Corinne looks at him over the pad, and writes down something short.
“It’s nothing,” Debbie says. “It’s a girl in her kitchen with a website.”
“It’s a girl in her kitchen with a website and a tip line, and by tonight it’s three girls in three kitchens. We’ll come back to the march.”
“Totally,” says Skye.

The bread comes in a basket under a white cloth and goes around. Debbie takes none. Corinne takes a piece and tears it in two and leaves both halves on her plate. Skye takes one and sets it on hers and folds her hands. Jack takes one because his mother raised him.

“Two.” Corinne doesn’t look at him for this one. She turns the pad a few degrees toward Skye and reads it flat, a line item in somebody else’s budget: “Mobile Uploads. Eleven forty-eight p.m. Caption, *my friend from school*. Following an email at nine-forty that said, and I’m quoting myself, *everything down*.”
Debbie lays her pen across her pad. “Baby,” she says. “A *bed*.”
“I’ll take it down after lunch,” Skye says. “You’re right. Totally.”

“Also,” Corinne says, and turns the BlackBerry a few degrees toward him without picking it up, “your wall. You were tagged, so it’s on your wall, and your wall is public, by the way, and it’s in Ohio. A Rita Pallante would like to know whether your mother knows about this.” She reads it exactly. “Two question marks.”
Debbie turns to Jack with her hand on his sleeve again, low, confiding. “*Has* your mother seen it?”
“His mother,” Skye says pleasantly, before he can open his mouth, “is a very nice woman in Ohio, and she’s going to be fine.”
Ma is at her desk in the front office at St. Brigid’s right now with the late slips and the lost-and-found. He lets Skye have the answer.
The salads come, and the chicken, and the waiter comes back with the basket warm and sends it around again. Under the cloth Skye’s ankle rests against his, and her shoes stay on.

She eats what her mother eats, at her mother’s speed: a forkful of lettuce when Debbie takes one, the fork down when Debbie’s goes down. Debbie sees him noticing, and seems to take it for something else.
“She was the easiest kid,” Debbie tells him, fond, with the fork in the air. “Ask anybody. She never cried unless you asked her to.”
Skye laughs at that, right on time, and Debbie pats her hand.

Debbie laughs at something Corinne says — the carpeted laugh, warm to the walls — and Jack puts it now with something he only heard about: a phone on the back of a toilet on Del Playa at seven on a Friday morning, forty minutes of it, under a shower turned up as high as it goes. He heard about it at seventy miles an hour on Saturday. Now it’s across a tablecloth from him, asking if the chicken’s all right.
“Three,” Corinne says, and looks at Debbie, and Debbie picks this one up herself.

“The accountant called me Saturday,” she tells the table. “In Encino. On a *Saturday*. That man doesn’t know Saturdays exist.” She turns to her daughter, sweet as anything. “Twenty-five thousand dollars, sweetheart. On the phone. To a volunteer.”
“To Haiti,” Skye says.
“It’s tax-deductible,” Corinne says, writing, as if that were the least of it.
“It’s *Skylark*’s,” says Debbie.
“Skylark has a board,” Corinne tells Jack, by way of a footnote. “The board is her mother.”
“I’m Skylark,” Skye says.
Debbie reaches across the cloth and pats her daughter’s hand twice, fond and perfectly sure. “Sweetheart,” she says. “*I’m* Skylark.”
Corinne writes that down too, or something near it. Skye smiles at her mother, and picks up her water, and drinks a little, and sets the glass back on its own wet ring.

“Which brings us back,” Corinne says, “to the march.” The network called yesterday — not the publicity office; somebody two floors above it, very friendly — to ask whether Cassidy is pro-life now. A Christian blog with a cross in its banner has emailed to ask the same thing with more exclamation points, and to ask whether Skye would say a few words about her journey. Corinne circles *journey* on the pad and reads it out with no expression at all. “I’d like to know what to tell them,” she says, “before the trades do.”
Debbie turns her pen end over end on the pad. “Everybody marches,” she offers. “Marching is very in.”
“Option one.” Corinne reads it off the pad. “*Skye was there to support a friend.*”
“Friends,” Debbie says. “Plural. Friends is warmer.”
“Friends is vaguer.”
“Vaguer *is* warmer, Corinne.”
“Whatever you write,” Skye says, “I’ll say.”

She has agreed with everything said at this table since the bread. Corinne’s pen waits over the pad, and Debbie waits with it, and Skye sits across from the two of them with her hands in her lap, pleasant, ready to be told.

choices.key: At the lunch in Studio City you found Skye’s hand under the table. It was cold, and it didn’t hold back. You held it anyway.
response: He finds her hand under the cloth, in her lap, where she has it folded into the other one. It’s cold. It doesn’t hold his back. Every other time he has taken her hand it has done something in his — tugged, tapped out a rhythm, laced, pulled him somewhere — and this one only lies there, like something handed to him to hold.

He holds it anyway. He holds it all through the march question, through Corinne’s three possible statements and Debbie’s fourth, under the tablecloth where nobody can see, and Skye answers every one of them with the other hand, turning her water glass by the stem, *totally*, *that’s good*, *I like the second one*. Somewhere in the middle of the second statement her thumb moves across his knuckles, one time, and goes still again.

choices.key: At the lunch you asked Debbie about the Lumina, and gave Skye four minutes nobody was looking at her.
response: “Mrs. Callender,” he says, into the gap after the march question. “I’ve been meaning to ask you about the Lumina.”

Debbie lights up like a porch light. “’*Ninety-four*,” she says, and she’s off: a driveway in Simi Valley dressed up as Ohio, with fake leaves; a little boy actor who bit; nineteen takes of forgetting the same brown-bag lunch on the same car roof, and a director who kept saying *more mom*. She does the line for him. She half stands in the booth to do it, a hand flying to her cheek — “*Did I forget something?*” — and finds a mark on the carpet sixteen years old without looking down for it. Corinne actually puts her pen down to listen.
For four minutes the table is all Debbie’s, and nobody at it is looking at Skye. Skye is looking at him. She looks at him the whole four minutes.

choices.text: *Let her run it. She asked you to.*
choices.key: At the lunch you let Skye run it, the way she asked.
response: He keeps his counsel. It’s harder than he’d have guessed. The march question goes past him three times — Corinne drafting out loud, Debbie sanding the drafts — and every time he has the answer ready in his mouth, and every time he eats a piece of chicken instead.

He keeps watching the one place under this table nobody else at it would think to look. Once, across the bread basket, Skye’s eyes come to his — she has seen him keep the rule — and go back to Corinne before Corinne can see them go.

choices.key: At the lunch you broke Skye’s one rule and answered the march question yourself.
response: “She came because I was going,” Jack says.

Three faces turn. He keeps going; it’s short, and it’s true. “She argued with me for two miles. She’s not pro-life.” Corinne’s pen has started to move, so he says the rest to Corinne. “She’s pro-*me*.”
Corinne writes it down, every word, and underlines something. Debbie claps her hands together under her chin. “Oh, *write* that,” she says.
“I am,” says Corinne.
Under the table Skye’s foot finds his and comes down on it, hard, with the heel. It’s furious. It’s the first real thing she’s done all lunch, and above the tablecloth her face doesn’t move at all.

s08a.slug: TUESDAY · 1:50 PM · VENTURA BOULEVARD, STUDIO CITY — THE FAMILY MATTER
body: The waiter has crumbed the cloth with a little silver blade and taken everything but Jack’s plate, because Jack hasn’t finished. Debbie has a cappuccino she isn’t drinking. Corinne has an espresso and drinks it in one swallow, like a pill.
She slides her legal pad out from under the BlackBerry and turns it around on the cloth so it faces him, and takes the cap off her pen.
“At our last lunch,” she says, “I said there was a family matter we’d want to talk through at some point. And I said not today.” A small smile, fair as smiles go. “Today.”

There’s no manila folder this time. There are three printed pages clipped under the pad, and the top one has the *Vindicator*’s masthead on it, the paper’s website, printed in color off somebody’s office printer — the same masthead that landed on the porch on Glenwood Avenue every morning he was growing up. Corinne doesn’t read him the article. She reads him her own notes off the top sheet, in her small upright hand.
“Struthers, November 2007. Felonious assault. A plea in January 2008. Five years.”
She stops there and looks up. Beside him, Skye hasn’t moved.

Under the printout there’s a second page, a screenshot: a gray column of comments, two of them circled in red pen. “And this,” Corinne says. “Comment thirty-one called your brother a convict. Comment thirty-four is your sister calling comment thirty-one a name I had to look up.” She touches the second circle with the cap of her pen. Under it, at the bottom of the comment: *his SISTER.* “She signed it.”

She lays the pen down across the pad. “Here’s what I see from my desk,” she says. “A girl a network pays to be sweet. A march. A brother in a state prison. Right now those are three different websites. The day one of them puts all three in a sentence, I spend February on the phone.” She doesn’t look at Skye. “Two weeks ago somebody at this table told me to know it about somebody else’s family. I’d love to. This is the family in the picture.”
Across from him, Debbie takes her hand off her cup.

Jack puts his knife and fork together on his plate, squared, handles at four o’clock, the way Ma taught all of them to do it in restaurants so the waiter knows. The bread basket is still on the cloth, under its napkin. He doesn’t take any.
“Jack.” Corinne says it kindly; her voice doesn’t change, it only gets a little lower. “I’m not asking for the papers. I have the papers. What happened?”
“A fight,” Jack says. “A guy got hurt bad.”
Corinne waits, pen up, in case there’s a paragraph coming. He gives her what else is true.
“He took a plea,” he says. “I go see him. He’s the best man I know.”
“What’s his name?” Debbie says. It’s the first thing she’s said since the printout.
“Danny.”
“Danny,” Debbie says, as if she were putting it somewhere she would be able to find it again.
Corinne nods and doesn’t write any of that down.

Skye has been sitting through all of it with her hands in her lap and her face arranged, as it’s been all lunch. Now she takes the napkin off her lap, and folds it in half, and lays it beside her plate. She looks straight at Corinne.
“He’s at Trumbull Correctional,” Skye says. “A555218. I wrote him Thursday night. He hasn’t written back. I’m told it’s slow.”
Debbie turns and looks at her daughter.
“Skye,” Corinne says, gently, “it isn’t whether *you* care.”
“Then we’re done with it,” Skye says.

She says it pleasantly, and it doesn’t move. Corinne looks at her across the cloth. She turns the pad back around to face herself, and under her own notes, in the small upright hand, she writes the number down: A555218. She caps the pen.
A waiter comes to the end of the booth with the dessert menus, looks at the four of them, and goes away again with all of the menus.

“All right,” Corinne says. “Then here’s my job.” The item is out, so February is dead — the network thing, the photographer she likes standing by the valet; you can’t arrange to be seen for the first time by people who saw you on Monday. Instead: Thursday night. A fundraiser, at a house in the Palisades. “You arrive together. You’re photographed arriving together. You stay an hour, you’re charming, you leave.” She puts the BlackBerry back in her bag. “It’s a fundraiser. It’s *civic*.” And to Jack, dry as a cracker: “You’re not a friend from school anymore, by the way. You’ve been promoted. Wear the blazer.”
Jack doesn’t say anything. Nobody has said whose fundraiser, or what it’s for.
“Fine,” Skye says. It’s the morning’s fine again, every corner sanded off.

Out front the sun has gone over to the other side of Ventura, and the awning throws a hard green shade on the sidewalk. Skye is inside settling up with the black card — Skylark’s, not hers — and Corinne is at the curb with the BlackBerry at her ear, saying her own name to somebody. The valet takes Jack’s ticket and runs up the block toward the lot.

Across Ventura a man sits on a bus bench with a camera in his lap, a long lens on it, not waiting for any bus. Corinne has seen him. She has turned so that her back is to him, and so that she is between him and the door.

Debbie stands beside him at the podium with her sunglasses in her hand, not putting them on. She watches the restaurant door. Through the glass Skye is at the host stand with the check folder open, signing, laughing at something the host has said, the whole smile, for the host.
“Is she eating?” Debbie says. “Up there?”
“She eats.”

“Good.” A car goes by with its windows down and its radio loud, and is gone. “She wrote to your brother?” she says. There’s no lobby in it at all; it’s the Lancaster under the hotel, flat and level. “In prison?”
“Yes.”
“She doesn’t write to anybody.”
Up the block the Saab comes out of the lot and around the corner with the valet driving it like it’s his. Debbie watches it come.
“She doesn’t write to me,” she says.

The restaurant door opens behind them, and Skye comes out into the sun putting the black card away. Debbie puts her sunglasses on. By the time she turns around she has the lobby back in her voice, every bit of it, and her arms out.
“Text me when you’re home, sweetheart,” she says. “Drive like a person.”

journal.title: Debbie Callender
journal.text: Skye’s mother. Her manager. A voice like a hotel lobby. Did a Chevy commercial in ’94. Calls her baby. Keeps a legal pad. ‘Then you’re going to be very expensive.’ Tuesday, Studio City: already up, already asking about Teddy. ‘Baby. A *bed*.’ The accountant in Encino called her about Haiti: ‘Sweetheart, *I’m* Skylark.’ At the valet, with no lobby in it: Skye doesn’t write to anybody. She doesn’t write to her.

journal.title: Corinne Waxman
journal.text: Corinne Waxman. Skye’s publicist. Answers the phone with her own name. Reads a BlackBerry the way other people read a room; uses a legal pad only when a lawyer might read it later. Ran my name in January. Tuesday she read the *Vindicator* off it, and asked me, kindly, what happened. Wrote down Danny’s number when Skye said it. Thursday: a fundraiser in the Palisades. It’s civic.

s09.slug: TUESDAY · 3:20 PM · US-101 NORTH, CALABASAS → THOUSAND OAKS
body: She bought it before she’d pulled away from the curb: the entire record, on her phone, with the valet still standing at her window waiting on his tip. “It came out today,” she said, “and I needed something nobody’s heard yet.” Now it’s on in the Saab: a slow drum machine, a guitar that keeps circling one high bright figure, a woman’s voice somewhere far back in all of it, as if she were singing from the next room of a very big house.

body.text: At the bottom of the on-ramp, without looking at him, she said, “You broke the one rule.” A mile later: “*Pro-me.*” She didn’t say whether it was a complaint. She hasn’t said anything since.
At the bottom of the on-ramp she said, “Four minutes. You gave me four minutes of the Lumina,” as if she were reading a figure off a contract. She hasn’t said anything since.
She said nothing on the on-ramp. She said nothing through the Valley, either, past the Encino exits and the long beige walls of Tarzana and Woodland Hills.

body: It’s been twenty minutes of that. The freeway climbs out of the Valley at Calabasas into hills that went green in the rain and are still green, rough and bright, with red-tile roofs stacked up the slopes and a hawk sitting on a light pole. He doesn’t fill it. He watches the hills.

At Agoura, coming up on the Kanan Road exit, she reaches down without taking her eyes off the road and works one heel off with the toe of the other foot, and then the other one, and kicks both shoes under her seat. She drives on barefoot, her toes curled over the edge of the gas pedal. Her dress has ridden up past her knees for the driving, and she leaves it there.
“I’m very good at fine,” she says.
He waits.
“I do it in the car on the way. By the time the valet’s got my door I’m finished. You watched me do it from Montecito to Ventura.” She doesn’t look over. “You let me.”
He did.
“We don’t say fine in my house,” he says. “We say good. *How’s your father?* He’s good. *How’s Danny?* He’s good. *How are you, Jackie?* Good.” He watches the hills. “Good’s worse.”
She looks over at him for the first time since Ventura Boulevard, and back at the road.

“She’s my manager. She’s my mother. She did my taxes before I knew there were taxes. Skylark’s hers — she named it. She names everything. Her cars have names. Her plants have names.” “She’s named everything I’ve got.”

“She’s not a monster. Don’t make her one, I’ll know. She’s scared. They’re all scared — did you see it? Corinne’s scared of the network, and my mother’s scared of Corinne, and the network’s scared of a girl in a kitchen.” A truck downshifts beside them. “And I’m fine. I’m the only one at the table who’s fine.”
She passes a landscaping truck with three men asleep in the back of it.

“You know what’s in her downstairs bathroom? My first headshot. Framed. I’m nine. I’m holding a puppy and laughing my head off.” She checks the mirror. “It was the photographer’s puppy. I had it for twenty minutes. It peed on me. Every person who’s ever used that bathroom has looked at me loving a dog I didn’t have.”
“What was its name?” Jack says.
“The photographer never said.” She almost smiles at the road. “So I named him. Pancake. For twenty minutes in 1999 he was Pancake, and that was mine.”
“I told you about the shower,” she says. “I didn’t tell you I still do it. I did it Sunday night.”

She breathes out through her nose, a long one, and the next thing she says is nearly a joke. “Thursday I’m going to be civic.” She tries it again, bigger. “I’m going to be *so* civic, Jack. I’m going to be civic all over the Palisades.” He laughs, and she looks pleased with herself for the length of an overpass.
She asks him nothing about Danny. She didn’t through the Valley, and she doesn’t now.
He tells her one thing anyway.

“He prints,” Jack says. “Danny. Every letter, big block letters, pressing so hard you can read it from the back of the page. Like he’s yelling it across the yard.” Westlake goes by. “When he writes back, you’ll know it’s him from the envelope.”

She doesn’t answer. She eases off the gas, and the Saab comes down a little under seventy. At the Westlake Boulevard exit she says, “Block letters,” quietly, to herself, trying it, as she tries a line she likes. Thousand Oaks starts up ahead of them in the haze.

choices.text: “You weren’t fine. Your shoes were on.”
choices.key: In the car you told Skye her shoes were on at lunch. She laughed, and was furious that you knew.
response: She turns and looks at him at seventy miles an hour, for longer than he’d like.

Then she laughs out loud, and she’s furious, and says so. “You’re not allowed to know that. Nobody’s allowed to know that. *I* didn’t know that.” She hits the horn at nobody, one long blast, and a man in a Camry looks over at them. “Shoes,” she says to him, through the glass, and waves.

choices.text: “You came back. For Danny. I saw.”

s09a.slug: TUESDAY · 4:05 PM · US-101 NORTH, THE CONEJO GRADE
body: Past Newbury Park the freeway comes up over the top of the Conejo Grade, and the Oxnard plain opens out below them all at once: flat and green to a brightness at the far end that has to be the sea, fields laid out in long rows under white plastic, lines of eucalyptus standing up out of them for windbreaks, Camarillo in the middle distance, and the sun gone low and gold over all of it, coming in sideways through the windshield. The grade drops away in front of them. In the right lane the trucks are down in low gear, groaning, and at the bottom of the hill the northbound lanes are a red string of brake lights as far as Jack can see.
Skye takes the Saab down into it, braking and letting off. The record is still on, low.
Inside his jacket the RAZR goes off against his ribs, and again, and twice more.

body: He shuts the phone. Ahead of them a horse trailer with nobody’s horse in it brakes, and Skye brakes, and the Saab rocks on its springs and stops.
The RAZR hasn’t been shut a minute when it goes again in his hand, ringing this time, and the little outside screen says GLENWOOD.
Skye reaches over and turns the record off. In the quiet the Saab is all engine and tires, and the hiss of the car beside them, and a talk station coming out of somebody’s open window two lanes over.
He opens it. “Hi, Ma.”
“Jackie.” Not *hi, honey*. Not *did you eat*. “Are you driving?”
“No, Ma.”

“Good.” Behind her a cupboard door shuts. He knows where she is without being told: at the kitchen phone with the dish towel over her shoulder, the dinner done and the dishes done, because she would do the dishes first. “Rita Pallante called during dinner,” she says. “I didn’t get up. She called back.” Another cupboard. “She had a lot to say. I let her say it. I said, *Thank you, Rita*.”
A car horn somewhere down the grade, long, and then let go of.
“So I went down the basement to look, and Rosie was already at the Dell.” She breathes in. “She asked me did you get married.”

He can see it from here: the card table at the bottom of the cellar stairs, Pop’s Browns calendar on the wall over it, and Rosie in Ma’s chair in front of the screen, seven years old, swinging her feet. And tomorrow at twenty to eight Ma will be at the office window at St. Brigid’s with the lunch envelopes, and the mothers will come to the window one at a time, and every one of them will have seen it.

Beside him Skye has both hands on the wheel, high up, and the Saab is creeping in the brake lights. There’s nowhere in a car this size to take a phone call, and he doesn’t try to find one. He doesn’t turn to the window. He keeps the side of his face to her, and keeps his voice down, for her and for the car.
“I’m not going to ask you what that is,” Ma says.
The brake lights ahead of them go out in a long row and come on again. Skye’s right hand comes off the wheel to the gearshift, and takes it down a gear, and goes back up where it was.
“Saturday I said *that’s something*,” she says. “I meant it.”
“Gina showed me her. In the pictures from the march.”
“And then tonight —” she says, and that isn’t how it goes. “Your father —” And that isn’t it either, and she leaves it wherever she left it. He hears her take a breath to try it a third way.
“Jackie —”
And she stops.
