s09b.slug: TUESDAY · 4:12 PM · US-101 NORTH → THE LAS POSAS ROAD EXIT
body: “Tomorrow,” he says.
“Good,” Ma says. And then, in the same voice, without changing it: “And now the other thing.”
“What other thing?”
“I heard it when you said *hi, Ma*.” Not sharp. A woman reading something off a list she didn’t write. “You might as well say it. I already heard it.”
He looks at the brake lights. There’s nowhere in a car this size to say it, and he says it anyway, low, in the voice he keeps for her, with the side of his face to Skye.
“I think she’s the answer, Ma.”
Skye’s eyes come off the road to his face, and go back.

Ma doesn’t say anything at all. And into the quiet on Glenwood Avenue, through the kitchen wall, from her chair in the front room, comes Nonna: the rosary in Italian, both halves of it herself, steady and unhurried, loud enough that it comes down the line from Ohio and into a Saab on the 101. *Santa Maria, Madre di Dio, prega per noi peccatori.* It’s Tuesday. She’ll be on the Sorrowful Mysteries. *Adesso e nell’ora della nostra morte.* She starts the next one without stopping for breath, and Ma doesn’t cover the phone.

He has knelt on that carpet beside that chair since he was small enough to be eye level with the beads. He knows which bead is the chipped one. He holds the phone against his ear and listens to her go around.
“Your grandmother heard us,” Ma says.
The Saab rolls, and stops.
“Go tomorrow, Jackie.”
She hangs up gently — the small click of a phone being put back where it lives by somebody careful not to wake the house — and Glenwood Avenue is gone.
He shuts the RAZR and holds it on his knee.

The grade has let them down onto the flat. The fields go by on both sides under their plastic, rows and rows of them, and in one of them a crew in hooded sweatshirts is bent over the beds in the low sun with a truck idling at the end of the row. The brake lights thin out, and a green sign comes up out of the glare: LAS POSAS RD, the next exit. Skye puts her blinker on.

She takes the exit and pulls onto the shoulder of the ramp, short of the light, and stops there with the blinker still going. She takes the white iPhone out of the cup holder. He watches her thumb. Her own page, Mobile Uploads, and there it is at the top of the album. She doesn’t look at it long. Her thumb finds the place to delete it, and the phone asks her if she’s sure, and her thumb tells it.

She puts the phone back in the cup holder. She hasn’t said a word since his phone rang, and she doesn’t say one now. Jack doesn’t either. He keeps his hands on his knees. The ramp and the light and the thumb are hers.

She checks her mirror and pulls off the shoulder, through the light, around and onto the on-ramp north, and the blinker keeps on through all of it, until at the top of the ramp the wheel comes straight and puts it out.

journal.title: Ma
journal.text: Maria Costigan. St. Brigid’s school secretary. Feeds anybody who comes through the door. Cries at grace every year. Took my phone at the table and counted to eleven without looking at it once. Wrote Becca. December 6th, back from Trumbull: the November bill, four hundred and nine texts. Who is it. I told her a girl. Not Lena. Not nice — something. That’s what Dad said about her. Christmas week: took forever at the machines at Trumbull so Danny and I could talk. Stood Becca’s card at the front of the mantel. Brewed the New Orleans coffee Christmas morning. Put unlimited texting on the family plan; it was cheaper than me. Saw the photos. “Is she Catholic, at least?” When Danny laughed on the phone, she looked at me. Holy Family Sunday she took Pop in. ‘You sit, Frank.’ Showed him the machines. Goes to the seven o’clock on the last day of every year; this year I went with her. Lena called the house on the second of January, and Ma answered, and they talked for ten minutes. ‘She wants you. I don’t know why.’ Now she knows the coffee was hers. At the door she gave me the can back, empty, for the girl who called. From a gas station in Buellton I called her before I said yes on Skye’s phone. She said I was on the phone with Lena all break. I told her Lena’s still got a boyfriend, and he wrote her a song, and it was good. She didn’t say anything. Tuesday Mrs. Pallante called during dinner, and Rosie found it on the Dell before Ma got downstairs. She asked if we got married. Ma didn’t ask me what it was. She asked when I last went to confession. I said tomorrow. Then she said she’d already heard the other thing, when I said hi, so I told her: I think Skye’s the answer. Nonna heard us through the wall. ‘Go tomorrow, Jackie.’

s10.slug: TUESDAY · 5:50 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, THE PORCH — THE SWING
body: The sun has been down half an hour, and the sky over the Channel has gone the deep clear blue that comes after, with one long rag of pink over the islands going out. The porch light isn’t on yet. Down at the end of the street the surf is loud at the bottom of the bluff.

She drove the rest of the way home with the record off — through Ventura, and along the Rincon in the last of the sun with the surfers coming in off the water, and up through Carpinteria with her left hand on the wheel and her right hand in his on the console, where she put it at the county line and didn’t take it back. At the curb she popped the trunk and handed him the Carhartt, still folded, without a word about that either.

The swing is up. While they were in Studio City somebody hung it: the driftwood seat Sol has been sanding since the tornado, sanded so pale it holds the last of the light, on two lengths of new chain from the two hooks in the porch ceiling. Tomás’s drill is on the rail, and the coffee can of screws beside it, empty. Across the seat somebody has stuck a strip of masking tape and written on it in Tomás’s capitals: OILED 2 PM. SIT AT OWN RISK.

Sol is sitting on the top step with a bottle of beer when they come up the walk. She gets up. She sets her foot against the edge of the seat and gives the swing its first push, and watches it go out over the boards and come back on its chains, and nods at it. She collects her camera from the step and heads off down Del Playa toward the bluff, after whatever’s left of the light, and leaves them to it.

Skye peels the tape off the seat, folds it in half on itself, and hands it to Jack, and sits down on the swing. She sits at one end of the new seat with one foot under her and the other knee pulled up, her arms locked around it and her chin up, and the swing gives a little under her and settles.
“I took it down,” she says, as if he hadn’t been in the car.
He leans on the porch post.

“Corinne asked me on the phone at six in the morning. Then she asked me by email. With a subject line. With my mother cc’d.” The new chain creaks in its hook. “My mother asked me at lunch, with a pen. I said I’d take it down after lunch, and I meant after lunch next year. I’d have taken it down for Corinne never. I took it down for a woman I’ve never met, because of how you said *Ma*.”
She holds on to her knee. She’s braced, and he can see for what: for him to tell her it doesn’t matter, and for it to be the kind thing to say.

response: She looks at him from the swing for a long time, in the blue light, with the chain still creaking a little over her head.
Whatever she was braced against goes out of her arms. Her knee comes down, and her foot finds the boards.

So he tells her the true version, with nothing on it. He likes being with her. He likes how much fun it is, every day of it. The picture was the two of them, and it was true, and she doesn’t have to feel bad about putting something true where people can see it. He doesn’t care who saw it.
She watches him say it, every word, to the end. She nods, once.

response: He sits down next to her, and the swing takes his weight and goes back.
“Post anything you want,” he says. “Anything. I don’t care who sees it.”
She looks at him sideways, close, through the full arc back and the full arc forward, and on the way forward her hand finds his on the chain.

body: “I know. I can tell. I’m stopping anyway.”
He starts to say it again, and she shakes her head at him.
“You said *tomorrow* to your mother,” she says. “I know what tomorrow is.”
The swing goes back and comes forward. Somewhere down the street a screen door bangs and a girl yells somebody’s name at the beach.

“It costs you. Don’t tell me it doesn’t — I was in the car, I heard your half.” She looks up at the chains where they go into the ceiling. “And it costs me. With them.” She puts her foot down and stops the swing.

“And you told her I was the answer.” She says it to the chains. “On the Conejo Grade. In the brake lights. With me right there, with both hands on the wheel, being furniture.” Her thumb finds the seam of the driftwood and goes along it. “I’ve been the answer to a nine o’clock problem on Thursdays. I have never once been anybody’s answer to their *mother*.”

body.text: “Monday I made the good column. Today I’m the answer.” The swing goes back, and comes forward. “You keep promoting me, Jack. I’m going to need a bigger trailer.”

body: “I want your mother to like me. I want your grandmother to like me so much it’s stupid. I learned her prayer. I say it at red lights.”
“She’s had you in her rosary since Christmas,” Jack says.
Skye looks at him. “Me or Cassidy?”
“She’s working on it.”
“Tell her I’m available Thursdays at nine,” Skye says, against his shoulder. “Network permitting.”

Her head tips, and a smile comes up on her, bright and even, every tooth in it on its best behavior, and it’s Cassidy on the swing, Thursdays at nine, sweet as a church supper. “From now on,” Cassidy says, “only the nice ones.”

Cassidy goes as fast as she came, and Skye pushes them off again with her heel. “Pictures of you explaining things,” she says. “You explain things to people who didn’t ask. It’s the nicest thing about you. Your mother can look at that all day.”

He tells her about tomorrow, the rest of it. Hale is flying to New York on Thursday, so the Greene session has moved to his house, tomorrow at six, with the State of the Union on the television. Hale said to bring a guest.
“Come,” Jack says.

The swing goes back and comes forward while she thinks about it. “Go,” she says. “Bring me back Hale doing the President. I want all of it. I want his face in the applause breaks. If he heckles, I want the heckles word for word, and don’t clean them up, I’ll know.” She tucks her feet up under her on the seat. “I’m watching it here. Tomás and Sol. Tomás yells at the television on principle, and Sol films him doing it. So somebody can yell at it with me.”
She leans into his side, and he puts his arm along the back of the swing behind her, and they ride it like that until the porch light comes on over them by itself, on its timer.
He walks home up Del Playa in the dark, past the house parties starting up and a couch somebody has carried out onto a lawn to sit on, with his hands in his jacket and the RAZR quiet in one of them.
At the corner he looks back. Her porch is the one lit square on that side of the street, and the swing is still moving a little on its new chains — her on it, one heel on the boards, pushing off.

s11.slug: WEDNESDAY · 10:50 AM · ANACAPA COMMONS — THE TABLET
body: It is nowhere near lunch at the Commons, and the room is half full of people who have decided to be late for something. The television over the cereal bar is on CNBC with the sound off, a man in a tie explaining something to a ticker, and every few seconds the same four letters come around the bottom of the screen, AAPL, AAPL, the set stuck on a single name.
At the long table by the glass Theo has had the MacBook open to a live blog since ten, and he calls it aloud now, leaning into the turns. “And it’s *thin*. It’s thin, it’s thin, it’s —”
“How thin?” says Doug.
“Half an inch.”
“Of *what*?”
“A pound and a half. A nine-point-seven-inch screen. He has sat down in a chair to use it.” Theo’s hand goes to his chest. “The blog is moved.”
“The blog says the room laughed,” he goes on. “The blog does not say at what. The blog is as much in the dark as we are.”
“That,” says Margot, “is the most honest live blog ever filed.”
“And there’s a keyboard you dock it in. It *docks*, Pruitt. And it reads books.”
“Does it make calls?”
“It does not make calls.”
Doug takes this in as news of a death. “Then what is it *for*?”
“That is the beauty of it,” Theo says, with relish. “We have to be told.”
“Can you carry it in a backpack?”
“It’s a pound and a half, Pruitt. You could carry it in a handbag.”
“I don’t have a handbag.”
“You will.”
“It is a large iPhone,” says Margot, “that cannot make a phone call.”

“It reads books,” Kevin says. “It’s a Kindle that went to college.” He has found a napkin and begun long division on it. “Four ninety-nine for the cheapest one. That’s a semester of orgo books. The two books and the lab manual.” He studies the napkin, and the books lose, and he looks stricken to have caught himself at it.

At the far end of the table Priya has the orgo text open flat beside her tray to a page of hexagons; the highlighter is capped, and the page stays where it is. “Viewing of tonight’s address in the Fishbowl is sign-up only,” she tells the table, in case it is about to be a different kind of table. “Pruitt, you are on the list. In pen.”
“I love a list,” says Doug.

Skye is beside Jack with her coffee and her sunglasses pushed up into her hair, and her knee against his under the table, and she has been there since the Commons opened, saying almost nothing and, from the look of her, delighted by all of them — the look she gets around people who want nothing from her. She watches Doug’s face. When Doug, appealing at last to the one person present with a professional opinion, says, “Skye. You’re from Hollywood. What *is* it?” she doesn’t even look at the MacBook.
“It’s a placemat that knows things,” she says.
“*Dude*,” says Doug, with love.

The table has stopped treating her as a visit. Doug has given her his hash brown; Kevin has asked her, about Javi, whether Montana or Young; and Margot watches her with the sidelong suspicion she reserves for a sentence that is better than it has any right to be.
“The only open question,” Margot says, “is who will buy one and be ashamed.”
“I’d buy it if it came with a note from my mother saying I couldn’t,” Skye says.
Margot lowers the legal pad. It is as close as Margot comes to a standing ovation.
“You will hate it,” Margot tells Jack. “On principle.”
“I’ll hate it when there’s a Greene on it.”
“There is an iBooks,” says Theo.
“Then I’ll hate it in the same room as the Greene.” Skye steals the crust of his toast and eats it, looking at no one.
“Six o’clock, Costigan,” Theo says, over the lid. “I’ve pressed the blazer.”

Doug needs to know the size, so Jack takes a Commons tray off the stack and stands it on its end and frames a rectangle in the middle of it with his two hands — “About that” — and Doug leans in as if the rectangle might make a sound. The RAZR is lying open next to the syrup. Skye has the white iPhone out at arm’s length, back camera, blind, before he has finished the sentence.

Laney is at the next table over, behind Jack’s left shoulder, with a fruit cup and the pink BlackBerry face up beside it. Jack has the back of his chair to her. Skye, on his right, looks across his shoulder at the next table and gives it a small clear wave.

Laney spears a cube of cantaloupe. “Morning.”
Theo shuts the lid of the MacBook halfway, and says, at the volume of a back row: “You can’t know what a thing is *for*, Delaney, until somebody *tells* you.”
“Some people launch things without telling anybody, Theodore,” says Laney, “and everybody has to find out from the *internet*.”
Jack turns his head. They freeze: Theo with the lid at forty-five degrees, Laney with a cube of cantaloupe stopped on the fork in the air. Then they go on, worse.
“Which is why one waits for the facts, Delaney, before forming a view of the device.”
“I’ve been waiting for the facts since September, Theodore. Nobody sends them.”
“Perhaps the device is simply shy.”
“Shy.” Laney points the fork at him. “It walked out under a spotlight in front of the whole world and did a turn, Theodore. I have done that walk. That device is *scared*.”
“Of what?”
“Of being a phone.”
“Dude,” says Doug. “It *isn’t* a phone.”
Skye has leaned in to Jack’s ear with her coffee up in front of her mouth. “They’re running lines,” she says, low.
“What?”
“Those two. That’s blocked. Who’s the audience?”
“Me, apparently.”
She looks at him over the rim of the cup. “No,” she says. “You’re the B camera.” And drinks her coffee.

He pushes the little pitcher of milk across to her elbow before she has looked for it, and she takes it without comment. Doug asks Kevin whether the iPad has a camera, and Kevin says that it doesn’t, and Doug says that’s crazy, who’s it for, and the question goes around the table again.

Laney stands with her tray in one hand and comes by behind Jack’s chair on the way to the dish return. Her free hand comes down on his shoulder, finds the collar of his other flannel — the Walk one lives on Del Playa now — turned up on the left, and flattens it with one smooth pass of her palm. She is two steps on before she stops. Her back goes rigid. She walks again, faster, and sets the tray on the belt hard enough to rattle the forks.
Jack puts a hand up to the collar. “Did Laney just —”

“It’s a very powerful dish return, Pruitt.”
Skye watches Laney all the way to the dish window, with interest.
Theo closes the MacBook the rest of the way and folds his hands on the lid. “Verdict, Costigan,” he says. “The tablet.”

body: He shuts it. Inside the screen door, on the mat, there’s a steel dog bowl with BERKELEY painted on the side in a careful hand, and it’s already a bowl full of phones. He lays his on top, on a pink BlackBerry he knows. Hale meets him inside the door in his shirtsleeves with a corkscrew. “Mr. Costigan. You’ve brought nothing,” he says. “I admire that in a guest. It’s so rare.”

Hale’s house is the one he remembers from the fall: books to the ceiling on every wall that isn’t window, the woodstove going in the corner, and the table, the six-panel door on its trestles, under a white cloth tonight with a loaf on a board, a wedge of something orange and a row of glasses that don’t match. Berkeley is asleep on his side on the Turkish rug. A small television sits on a stack of encyclopedias at the far end of the room, tuned to the Capitol with the sound down, where men in dark suits are filing in under a flag the size of a house. Evan is going round with a bottle. Caleb has a chair already; Yusuf has brought his coffee from the Commons in a paper cup, with the lid on.

Lena is already here. She’s at the bookshelves with Laney, who is her guest, and her copy of the Greene is on the cloth at a place in the middle of the door, with a full glass of Hale’s red beside it and a second chair pulled in close. She has her hair up with a pencil through the knot and the medal outside her sweater tonight, and he knows where she is in the room every minute without having to look.
When he comes in, her eyes go to the door and away. The curb heard him on Saturday, and he’d bet half of Newman has by now.

Theo comes up the walk at five to six in the pressed blazer with the bottle held out before him in both hands, and gives Hale the story on the step. It’s Monday’s story, and it has grown. The ambassador now has a name and a widowed sister in San Marino, and he wept, specifically, during the fish; the crate was stenciled in Logroño; the cellar in Pasadena is kept at fifty-five degrees by a man called Ignacio, who has been with the family thirty years and will not be rushed. Hale listens to all of it with his head on one side, turning the bottle in his hands.
“Mr. Vance,” he says. “There’s a price on it.”
“He was a humble man,” says Theo.
Hale gives it to Evan. “Open it. We’ll find out what humility tastes like.”

Laney has brought a Texas sheet cake in a Pyrex dish with the foil crimped down at the corners, still warm, because in Dallas, she informs Hale, you do not show up to a speech without a sheet cake. “Then the speech has already been improved,” Hale says, and takes the foil off himself. When Jack passes her at the shelves, Laney gives him a nod that would do for a stranger at a bus stop, and nothing else.

Somebody has been at the table before him. The sheet cake ends up in front of the place with Lena’s book, and Theo, coming past, takes the open Rioja back from Evan, sets it down in front of the chair pulled in beside it, and steers Jack toward that chair with a hand in the small of his back, talking about sediment.

Hale comes out of the kitchen with a stack of jam jars for the overflow and stops. He sets the jars down. He picks up Lena’s chair, carries it the length of the room to the far end of the door, and puts it down there; then he goes back for her book and her glass, and puts those down with it. “Opposite ends,” he says, to the room in general, “for the safety of the others.”

Lena sits down where he has put her without a word about it. Laney carries the sheet cake down after her. Jack takes the near end, by the screen door, and Theo takes the chair beside him with the expression of a director whose set has been struck by the landlord.
The President comes down the aisle at six through a crowd of people who want his hand, and Hale turns the sound up. “Ladies and gentlemen,” he says. “The warm-up act.”

It’s jobs first. “Sensible,” says Hale. “No politician ever lost a room by coming out against unemployment.” Next a freeze on spending, three years of it, everything but security. “A freeze,” Hale says. “In January. Somebody on his staff has been reading Dante.” Caleb laughs, late, and too loud for the size of the room.
At the far end Lena laughs too, before she can stop it, and puts the back of her hand to her mouth. He has to look at the television.

When the President gets to health care — Massachusetts, and not walking away from it now — Jack writes *Stupak?* in the margin of the Greene. At the far end of the door, without looking up, Lena’s pencil is moving on hers. He’d put money on the word. They’re agreeing about it at opposite ends of a door.

Every few paragraphs the chamber splits, half of it up on its feet and half sitting on its hands, and Hale points his glass at the half that’s sitting. “Say what you like about them. They are the only people in that room doing what they actually think.” Then at the half that’s standing: “And those are the only people in it who will get anything done. That is democracy, and you are welcome to it.”

The President turns at the podium and speaks to the Court. The justices are down in front in their black robes, and he tells them, more or less to their faces, that last week’s decision has thrown the doors open to special interests, foreign money among them, and the room comes up on its feet around them. The camera finds one justice sitting still in the middle of it, and his head goes side to side, and his mouth makes the shape of *not true*.
“Oh, *dear*,” says Hale, enchanted. “A justice with an opinion. In public. The cheek of the bugger. In England we’d have him stuffed.”

When the speech comes round to Afghanistan — the troops, and when they’ll start to come home — Yusuf’s coffee is on its way down to the table, and it stops halfway and doesn’t go the rest of the way. Hale keeps his mouth shut through all of it.

Laney has been cold to him all evening, which for Laney takes work. At the half hour she goes up the side of the door with a knife, cutting the sheet cake and leaving a slab of it on a napkin in front of everyone but him; and when Jack asks the table for the bread, the basket is at her elbow. She picks it up and holds it out to him with a little church-supper nod of encouragement, and her face catches up with her hand halfway across. She lets go of it so fast he nearly drops it.

Hale turns the television off at ten past seven, as the man from Virginia comes up in the corner of the screen. “Before the rebuttal,” he says, “which I refuse to dignify. He’ll be very reasonable, and I haven’t the stomach.” He pours for every glass that’s held out to him, and two that aren’t, and sits back down midway along the door, and lays the novel on the cloth in front of him.

s13.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:12 PM · HALE’S, THE DOOR ON TRESTLES
body: “Nineteen forty-four,” says Hale. “A flying bomb comes down by the Common. Bendrix is on the stairs when it lands, and the front door comes off its hinges and down on top of him, and he’s out cold under it.” He knocks twice on the panels in front of him. “You’ll forgive the furniture. Nobody has died under this one yet.”

“Sarah sees him under it and thinks he’s dead. So she kneels on the floor and makes a promise to a God she doesn’t believe in: let him be alive, and she’ll give him up. And in he walks, with plaster in his hair.” Hale opens his hands. “She keeps it. She ends the affair without a word of why, and he finds out two years later from her diary, which a private detective steals for him. Greene’s little joke, of course, is that her mother had her baptized when she was small and never told her. The paperwork was in order all along.” He turns his head to the far end. “Was she right to keep quiet? Miss Broussard.”
Lena doesn’t open the book. She has his sentence by heart, and she says it down the length of the door, word for word:

“*A man who keeps quiet to save himself has already confessed; he’s only chosen the wrong confessor.*” Then: “You wrote that, Costigan. Sarah kept quiet to save herself — from having to hear him. She owed him one sentence. *I made a promise and I’m keeping it.* That’s all it would have cost her. Instead she let him walk around London for two years thinking he’d been thrown over, because one sentence would have meant an argument, and she didn’t trust herself to win it.” Her hand is on the cover of the Greene. “Aquinas puts truthfulness under justice. Second part of the second part, question one-oh-nine. It isn’t manners. It’s owed. The truth about a man’s life belongs to the man. You don’t get to keep it for him because it’s heavy.”
It’s good. It’s better than his was, and it’s his.
“She didn’t owe Bendrix the reason,” Jack says. “She made the promise to God. Not to him. What she owed, she owed to God, and she paid it.”
“God doesn’t need her to lie to a man to keep a promise.”

“She didn’t lie. She kept quiet.” He has the Penguin shut under his hand. “Next question over. One-ten. Your man says it’s lawful to hide the truth prudently, and he got that from Augustine. That’s two Doctors of the Church on my side of the door.”
“*Prudently*.” Lena lets it sit on the cloth. “Lord have mercy, Costigan. Prudently is for an afternoon. Not for two years while he goes out of his mind.”
Yusuf has his coffee in both hands. “Where I grew up,” he says, quietly, “a promise to God was nobody else’s business. You didn’t explain it. You kept it.”
“It’s somebody else’s business,” Lena says, not unkindly, “when it’s his life you promised away.”
Hale turns his head back to the near end, and the room turns with him.

choices.text: “A vow you explain is a vow you’ve put up for negotiation. He’d have talked her out of it. He’s a novelist. He’d have won.”
response: “So she lied to him,” Lena says, “to keep from losing an argument.” She lets the table hear how that sounds. “That’s not a vow. That’s a debate strategy. If he could have talked her out of it, it wasn’t much of a promise. And if it was, he couldn’t have. Either way she owed him the chance to try.”
He has an answer for that. It isn’t as good as hers, and he doesn’t use it.
“*There is a silence that isn’t cowardice: when the truth would only be one more thing taken from people who have already lost everything.*” He doesn’t need the page either. “You wrote that.”
Halfway down the door Caleb says “Oh,” out loud, and puts his hand over his mouth.
“Bendrix hadn’t lost everything,” Lena says. “He’d lost *her*.” Her pencil goes still on the cover. When she goes on, it’s lower. “It’s not the same.”

choices.text: “She owed him a sentence. You’re right.”
response: It throws her. She looks at him down the length of the door like a player whose opponent has moved a piece she didn’t see.
“Then what are you defending?”
He doesn’t know yet. He’s going to have to find out with Hale’s table listening.

choices.text: “She did tell him. She left. It was the only sentence he’d believe.”
response: “Leaving isn’t a sentence,” Lena says. “It’s a door.” She knocks once on the six panels of one.
If it’s a joke, she doesn’t give anybody time to laugh at it.

s13a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:20 PM · HALE’S, THE DOOR ON TRESTLES
body: “At least Sarah kept a diary,” Lena says. “In a drawer. In her own house. Parkis had to steal it to read it.” She lays the pencil down, long enough for the table to think she’s finished.
“Some people publish.”
It takes the room a moment to understand that she has left the book.
“Miss Broussard,” Hale says, mildly. “The text.”

“I’m on the text.” She doesn’t look at him. “Sarah wrote to God where nobody would ever see it. That’s what the diary *is*. The most private thing in the novel, and it took a thief to get it out of the drawer.”
“A website on Monday,” she says. “A bed on Tuesday. An iPad before lunch today.”
“And a car on Saturday night.”
“Picture it,” Theo says brightly, to the table at large. “A sorbet. Between courses. Something with lemon in it, to —”
“Mr. Vance is a guest,” says Hale, “and guests are seen and not bloody heard.”
Theo is seen. Lena looks down the door at Jack. “Your friend from school.”
“You don’t know her.”
“No,” Lena says. “I’ve been kept informed.”
So it reached her. All of it, a day at a time, out at the far end of campus, by whatever road these things take.

“It was a true picture,” he says. “She didn’t do it to anybody. She did it because she’s sick to death of being told what she’s allowed to have. And she took it down herself, yesterday, on the side of the freeway, the second she saw it cost somebody something. She did that on her own. She gave to Haiti before anybody called her and asked. She reads Chesterton on the beach and argues with him in the margins, and half the time she wins. She makes me say what I think, and then she argues with that. When she pretends, she lets me watch her do it. Nobody else gets to.”
Lena doesn’t interrupt him. She lets him get all the way to the end, and then she picks the pencil up off the Greene.
“I didn’t say she wasn’t real, Jack,” she says. “I said she publishes.” She turns the pencil end over end and lays it down. “The real ones you keep in a drawer.”

choices.text: “Greene published. Sarah’s diary *is* the book. You’re prosecuting the novel.”
response: Hale is half out of his chair with pleasure. Lena doesn’t look at him.
“Greene was a married man writing about his mistress, Costigan,” she says, flat. “He’d know about publishing.”
It goes in under something, and she doesn’t wait to see where.

choices.text: “And some people date a man who agrees with everything they say.”
response: It wins the point. He hears it win.
Beside him Theo sets his glass down. At the far end Lena takes the full glass she hasn’t touched and pushes it away from her across the cloth, slowly, until it’s out of her reach.
On Sunday night he told Theo to stop kicking that man. He has just put the boot in himself, in front of a table, and it doesn’t feel like anything he wanted.

choices.text: “Fine. Sarah’s diary was in a drawer.”
response: She doesn’t take it.
“Don’t do that,” she says, quietly. “Don’t give me the drawer.”

choices.text: *Don’t take the bait. Back to Greene.*
response: He goes back to the book instead, to the end of it, where his side lives.
She lets him go. She folds her arms on the Greene and waits for him there.

s13b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:28 PM · HALE’S, THE DOOR ON TRESTLES

body.text: She doesn’t answer the shot. She hasn’t looked at him since it landed; she is looking at the novel.
“Go on, then,” she says. “Defend the ending.”

body: He goes to the ending.

“Sarah dies,” he says. “That’s the part people forget, because by then the book’s about something else. She dies, and what Greene leaves you is the two men. Bendrix and Henry — the lover and the husband. Two men who lost the same woman, living in the same house, walking across the Common to the pub together at night.” He has the Penguin open to the last pages, though he doesn’t need it. “That’s the end. They end up friends. Good friends. Bendrix hates God on the last page and can’t stop talking to him, and he has Henry. That’s what grace looks like in Greene. It’s what’s left when you can’t have the other thing. You get to be friends.”
At *friends* she looks up. At *good friends* her chair goes back, and she’s on her feet, and her hand comes down on the door.
“If we’re such *good friends*,” she says, “how come I had to find out about your girlfriend from a Facebook status, when we talked every single day for weeks leading up to it?”
It isn’t a big room, and she fills it.

Theo’s hand stops on the neck of the bottle. Beside her, Laney has the cake knife still in her fingers and her face wide open. Caleb doesn’t move. Hale doesn’t move. On the Turkish rug Berkeley, who can’t hear a thing, lifts his long gray head off his paws: the door jumped.
*Every single day.* He’d have said most nights, if anybody had asked him. She has it as every day.
Jack looks down the length of the door at her, and there is nothing in his mouth. He goes through himself for an answer fast, pocket by pocket, and comes up with nothing he can say at this table.

choices.text: “You should have heard it from me.”
choices.key: At Hale’s, Lena asked why she had to find out about your girlfriend from a Facebook status. You told her she should have heard it from you. It wasn’t an answer.
response: “Yes,” she says. “I should have.”
Her hand is still on the door. She waits, down at the far end of it, with Hale’s table waiting along with her, and nothing else comes. At last she takes the hand back.

choices.key: At Hale’s, Lena asked why she had to find out about your girlfriend from a Facebook status. You said nothing.
response: He says nothing. She gives him all the silence he could want to put something in, and he puts nothing in it.
In the corner the woodstove ticks.

choices.text: “It was a big month for Facebook.”
choices.key: At Hale’s, Lena asked why she had to find out about your girlfriend from a Facebook status. You made a joke. It died.
response: It dies in the air over the sheet cake. Caleb, who would laugh at anything tonight, doesn’t.
She doesn’t dignify it. She doesn’t even look up.

choices.key: At Hale’s, Lena asked why she had to find out about your girlfriend from a Facebook status. You started to say you didn’t know how, and stopped.
response: He stops. The end of the sentence is the thing he can’t say, and he hears the place in the air where it would go.
She waits exactly as long as it takes to be sure it isn’t coming.

s13c.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:33 PM · HALE’S, THE DOOR ON TRESTLES
body: It’s Hale who moves, and he does it gently; it’s the only rescue he’s got. “Sarah, Miss Broussard?”
“Sarah,” Lena says, and sits down.

She finishes on the book, at an ordinary volume, to Hale. “Sarah wasn’t cruel because she left him. People leave. She was cruel because she let him believe he’d been replaced. Two years. He paid a man to follow her around London and read the reports at night, which houses she went into, how long she stayed, and he hated some man he’d never met. Henry thought it was a man too. Parkis thought so. Everybody did. She let every one of them believe the cheapest thing there was, because the true thing was harder to say.” She closes the Greene. “She let him think it was a man.”
In the corner the woodstove ticks.
*Replaced.* Jack hears it, and the word stays on the cloth where she put it.

body.text: She looks at him once, at the end, down the whole length of the door, and it isn’t a win, on her face or on his.
Hale reaches for the bottle instead of a pen. At the far end Lena lays her pencil across the closed Greene. The point is hers, and she doesn’t look up from it.

body: Hale doesn’t try to start it again.

She’s up first. She takes her coat off the back of the chair, and Laney is up with her, leaving the Pyrex where it is with half the cake still in it, and the two of them come the length of the room on the far side of the door from him. At the screen door Lena finds her phone in Berkeley’s bowl without having to look and goes out onto the step.
Laney stops in the doorway beside Theo’s chair with the pink BlackBerry in her hand and says it low, down to him, where Jack can hear it perfectly well.
“Sugar, that was not about a *book*.”
“No,” says Theo.
The screen door slaps behind her. Theo is still holding the Rioja by the neck, with the price sticker turned into his palm.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. I told her what Danny asked about the third. If Pop won’t get out of the truck, she says, I get in. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. She asked if I asked Ma who the candle was for. No. You don’t. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks. I know what that means. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it. New Year’s Day I called her from the garage at the half, and she said, You called *me*. Saturday night she called the house — Ma answered and talked to her for ten minutes. Two hours on the kitchen phone, her mother’s cordless dying twice. Her grandmother made the christening gown for Luc in 1985; it rode out the storm in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. She had me be the priest so she could practice the promises. She thinks Binx doesn’t stop looking — he stops looking by himself. I told her Danny asked me something I can’t answer yet; she didn’t ask what. She asked how California was. ‘Come back, Youngstown.’ Two hours, and she never said Julian’s name. Lucille was baptized in the third quarter, and she didn’t get one word wrong. After that I called every night. Twelfth Night she got the baby in the king cake. Friday she said she hasn’t been fair to Julian, and she’s going to fix it. Sunday she landed: come find me tomorrow. Monday I couldn’t find her — not at 217, not at the twelve-ten. She came into Hale’s seminar a step behind him with a king cake, and the only chair left was next to mine. She was polite to me for fifteen minutes. Then Dido. Tuesday morning Julian put up a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late. She’s tagged. She’d said call me after. I didn’t. At the mailboxes she asked about my break, and I told her as far as Denver, and Ma’s words about the coffee. ‘Tell her I’m glad.’ The baptism was lovely. Tuesday night at St. Brendan’s she had the whole thing organized by half past eight, in a whisper, and put me on the table with Becca. When the TV said trapped she left the room. Julian went. Wednesday at the table she met Skye. She said no pictures at the table, and I argued with her about it in front of everybody. That night at the desk: Skye’s envelope was the biggest. ‘Tell her thank you. From Newman.’ Thursday she took the far end of Hale’s table before anybody got there. She moved the Saints to Sully’s. Saturday in the back hall she said she changed her mind, and stood up for Laney, and said Skye gave a good performance, and wouldn’t say what she meant. At Atlanta she kept my chair till the half. At ten after three she told me the time. Wednesday at three in the morning, the aftershock, in the Fishbowl: she said I could stop whatever I’m doing. I don’t know what I’m doing. Thursday Hale read her whole name off his list. She told him Lena. Saturday she ran the van to San Francisco. Six hours, row three. She asked me if I was happy. I said yes. At the end of the Walk I asked her how she had the nerve to be mad at me. She didn’t answer. She thanked me for coming and left. Monday, when Caleb said I was on a blog, she turned a page. Hale gave her Sarah Miles to prosecute and me Sarah to defend. Wednesday at his house, with the President on, she didn’t drink her wine. A website on Monday, a bed on Tuesday, an iPad before lunch — she had the whole week. She said she had to find out about my girlfriend from a Facebook status, when we talked every single day for weeks. I didn’t have an answer. Sarah let him think it was a man, she said. She walked home up Del Playa with Laney.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’ MLK Day he shoveled sand one-handed for Sigma Rho with Hollis in the other. At midnight Wednesday he pitched me a movie about a man whose friend got dumped and was with somebody else in a week. He said it twice. Hollis made his week. Theo’s in. He’s keeping the egg. Saturday he became a brother. Sunday he runs. He was correct to Lena for seven hours at Sully’s and sent me the end of it. He started on Julian, and I told him to stop. Monday he asked me, hypothetically, where a man who doesn’t go to Sully’s watches the Super Bowl. Made himself my plus-one to Hale’s, with a bottle that had a story. Tuesday morning I told him I think she’s the answer. He wanted a pamphlet, framed. Then he said nobody ever asked her to be that, and an answer is heavy for the person you hand it to. At Hale’s door Laney told him that wasn’t about a book. He said no.

s14.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:37 PM · HALE’S DECK — THE BLUFF
body: He goes out through the slider onto the deck, because it’s the only door in the house that doesn’t lead past anybody. The fog hasn’t come in. The moon is high and white, nearly full, and at the foot of the bluff the surf is loud in the dark. The bench at the rail is wet. The last time he was out here she was on it, with the dog’s head in her lap. He doesn’t sit on it.

The deck turns the corner of the house, and from the corner he can see a long way up Del Playa under the streetlights. Two of them are walking up the middle of the lane, Laney’s arm through Lena’s. Halfway up, a garage on the ocean side has its door rolled up and its light on, and a guitar case leaning in the doorway; they walk past it and don’t go in. Jack watches them until the lane bends and there is only the lane.

Somewhere at the back of his head a song starts up, one he knows the name of, and he stops it at the first line. The ends of his fingers are going on the rail, the way they went at the curb on Saturday.
Out past the end of the cliff, across the black water, the old Point Marisol Light shows no light at all.

The slider rolls behind him. Hale comes out with a glass in one hand and the RAZR in the other, and puts the RAZR in Jack’s hand. “The only one in the bowl that folds,” he says. Jack puts it in his pocket without opening it. Hale goes to the rail a few feet down and stands there looking at the water, not at Jack, and doesn’t mention the last half hour. After a minute he holds the glass out sideways. Jack shakes his head, and Hale drinks it himself.
“I have to be somewhere at eight,” Jack says.
“Where,” says Hale, “does a Catholic go at eight o’clock on a Wednesday?”
“Where do you think?”
Hale looks out at the moon over the water. “Give him my regards,” he says. “He blessed my dog.” He takes his glass back inside.

It finds Jack at the rail as soon as he’s alone: first at the back of his mouth, then in his hands. The pack is in the inside pocket of the Carhartt with the lighter. The tin is in the other pocket, where it has ridden since Christmas.
The last one was after midnight on Saturday, on the low wall under the olive tree at St. Brendan’s, with the van’s engine cooling.
Through the glass behind him Evan is stacking jam jars in Hale’s sink.

choices.key: On Hale’s deck, after the fight, you lit one.
response: He lights it with his back to Hale’s window, cupping the lighter against the wind off the water. The first pull is everything he wanted out of it; the rest is only smoke, and he smokes it anyway, down to the filter, watching the surf come white out of the dark.
He puts it out on the wet rail and pockets the end, and at five to eight he goes down the deck stairs to the lane, late, smelling of it, on his way to confession.

choices.key: On Hale’s deck, after the fight, you put the pack back.
response: He takes his hand out of the jacket empty and puts both hands on the rail, where the salt has left it wet, and leaves them there until his fingers have forgotten what they were after.
At five to eight he goes down the deck stairs to the lane, fast and late, with nothing lit.

choices.key: On Hale’s deck, after the fight, you counted her eleven.
response: He takes the tin out instead and opens it on the rail, in the light from Hale’s window, for the first time this year. RELIQUARY, in her hand, on the lid.

He counts them with a fingertip and gets eleven, and counts again in case, and gets eleven. Same as December. He shuts it and puts it away, and at five to eight goes down the deck stairs to the lane, late.

s15.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:20 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S — BEHIND THE SCREEN
body: Del Playa is twenty minutes uphill to Ocean Road if you don’t stop, and he doesn’t. At Sol’s the porch light is on over the new swing, hanging from its two chains with a blanket folded over one arm of it; through the screen door the television makes a blue square on the front-room ceiling, and Tomás, with the whole of his lungs, is telling the pundits what they can do with their panel. Jack doesn’t slow down. Ocean Road, and the hill, and the A-frame coming up out of the dark with the olive tree over the courtyard wall, and at the back of the nave, behind the blue glass, the little light over the closet door.

At the doors he dips his fingers in the font and the water is colder than the night. Mrs. Fitch is at the card table inside, under one lamp, Sunday’s bulletin spread under it, the diocesan clip-art binder open to ANGELS and a pot of rubber cement at her elbow. The clock over the choir loft says twenty past. Mrs. Fitch has seen it too, and writes nothing in the ledger, which is its own sentence.
“Mr. Costigan.” She holds a cut-out dove up to the lamp, finds it wanting, and lays it down. “My granddaughter showed me your picture on the computer.”
“Which —”

“I didn’t ask which.” She finds the next dove. “At my age one stops asking which. I said a Hail Mary for the pair of you last night, and I expect to say one tonight. Tyler Brandt wants to start a novena. I told him a novena requires the consent of the subject, and he has taken it up with Father.” She lifts the plastic wrap off a plate at her elbow and holds it out. “Lemon bars are Sunday. This is Wednesday. You’ll have one anyway.”

“Father has been in there since eight,” she adds, and trims a wing. “He said, *If Mr. Costigan comes, I am here*, and went in, and I told him it was Wednesday and nobody comes on Wednesday. He said that was the point of Wednesday.”
He has one. It is cold and sharp and exactly as good as Sunday’s.

body.text: Her nose lifts a degree toward the Carhartt and comes down again. A second lemon bar arrives on his napkin without comment.

body: The index card on the closet door says KNOCK (GENTLY) in her hand. He knocks gently. On the far side, a string of wooden beads stops clicking against the arm of a chair.

The closet is the closet: the kneeler, the linen screen, the hooks from 1962, the Prodigal Son tacked up inside the door at the height of a kneeling man’s eyes, the father already running. Out at the card table Mrs. Fitch has begun to cut, steadily, a good deal louder than a dove requires.
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It’s been eleven days since my last confession.”
“Eleven days.” Osei says it back to him. “You are twenty minutes late, and I have said a great deal of the rosary. In Kumasi we say the one who arrives late has at least set out. Tell me.”

He tells it in the order it happened, in the short words a Catholic uses. He keeps the verbs honest, as he has since December: *I went*, and *I stayed*, and *I let it*, never *it happened*. The Saturday night of the sixteenth, straight from this closet to her room. Friday afternoon, in the daylight, with the blind up: everything but the one thing.
Saturday night, in a car at Pismo, where he stopped keeping count and a gearshift stopped him.

Monday at noon, her room, an hour before a seminar: he went up her stairs meaning to, and on her mattress he would have, and he wasn’t the one who stopped it. She stopped it, for Sunday. And after she had stopped it he lay under her and let her tell him what Sunday would buy, and wanted every word of it, and that goes on the list too. And that his mother found out from a picture, and asked him one question, and he said *tomorrow*, and through the wall his grandmother said the rosary, loud enough to come down the line, and here it is.

body.text: And one more thing from Monday, because it was said in Osei’s name, and Osei ought to hear what was done with it. She asked him whether he’d stay away from her if Father told him to. He said no. And then he told her Father wouldn’t. He gave her last fall’s question through this same linen, and *change the hour*, and went on past where Osei had stopped — that what’s good between two people is nothing you have to run from, and the bad doesn’t cancel it out. “I spoke for you, Father. I told her what you’d say. I don’t know if I had the right.”

body: “That’s all of it, Father.” And because it is true, and he has been carrying it since the walk up: “I knew when I went that I’d be in here tonight.” And because that sounds like the worst of it, and isn’t, he gives Osei the rest. “It’s not that I don’t care what it is. I do. I think she’s the answer, Father.”
The scissors stop. The church is quiet to the altar lamp, and the chair on the far side of the screen takes the leg, and Osei is quiet longer than he has ever been quiet in here.
“You think she’s the answer,” Osei says at last. “To what question?”

He has two of them in his pocket. He has had them since Christmas, his grandmother’s over her beads and his brother’s across a steel table, and he opens his mouth on the linen to give Osei one, and finds the place in the sentence where it would go, and nothing comes to stand in it.
Osei lets the nothing sit there long enough for both of them to hear it.

“Then find the question,” he says, “before you hand anyone the answer.” The beads move once. “And on the walk home, notice this, because you told it to me yourself: on Monday it was she who kept your Sunday, and not you.”

body.text: “And you spoke for me on Monday. I will not scold you for it. You were mostly right. I prescribed daylight, and you took it — on Friday with the blind up, and on Monday at noon with the door shut. I have seldom seen a prescription followed so exactly and to so little effect. The rest I will sign. What is good between you is good; God made it, and a man does not run from what God made. Whatever you have been calling her in here, the near occasion was the room, and the hour, and the door. And your last sentence is your own, but it is true: the bad does not cancel the good. Remember that the good does not cancel the bad either. Each is real, and each is answered for, here, by its name.”

“So hear what you have done tonight with the good. You have made her an answer. A man with an answer goes to it whenever the question aches, at any hour, behind any door. That is how a good woman becomes an occasion, Jack. And the doing would be yours, not hers.”

body: “You have brought me this same afternoon before, my friend, with another date on it. The door will be open next week, and God is not tired of you. But the screen is linen, Jack. It is not a curtain you draw between one Saturday and the next.” The chair. “When a man came back every week with the same broken wrist, we did not set it harder. We asked about the staircase.”
“Your mother asked you the right question. Most mothers ask the wrong one.”

Jack looks at the picture on the door, because it is at his eyes: the father with his robe gathered up, running, and a long way down the road the son, small, with his head down. The chair has stopped creaking. “When you leave here,” Osei says, “what is different?”

choices.text: “I want to. I don’t know if I can.”
choices.key: In the closet you told Father Osei you want to change and don’t know if you can. He said that’s further than wanting to want.
response: “I want to,” Jack says. “I don’t know if I can.”
His forehead is nearly on the linen. It smells of starch and old incense and, faintly, of Osei’s soap, and moves a little when Osei leans toward it.

“On the Saturday before last you told me you wanted to want to.” The chair creaks, and something comes into the voice behind the linen that, in a less careful man, might be relief. “Wanting is further than wanting to want. It is not far. It is further.” A breath. “A man who wants to, and does not yet know if he can, is standing where the help gets in. Stay there.”

choices.text: “I’ll keep the line. I can’t promise more and mean it.”
choices.key: In the closet you promised Father Osei only what you could mean: the line. He told you to mean it when it costs something.
response: “I’ll keep the line,” Jack says. “I can’t promise more and mean it.”
It is the most he has, and he has put all of it on the kneeler where it can be looked at. On the far side the beads move once through a hand.

“Then promise what you can mean,” Osei says, “and mean it when it costs something. Tonight it is free. The church is empty, and the screen is linen, and everyone who ever swore anything to me in here swore it easily.” The chair. “Keep the line. I will thank God for every night you keep it. But a line is where you stop. It does not tell you where to walk.”

choices.key: In the closet you asked Father Osei to tell you what to do. He wouldn’t. He said you’d keep it better if it was yours.
response: “Tell me what to do, Father.”
He hears how it sounds as it leaves him, and leaves it there.

“No.” It isn’t unkind. “You will keep it better if it is yours. Whatever I handed you tonight, you would resent by Friday, and you would be right to.” The beads click once against the chair, and are still. “I will tell you one small thing, though. After the absolution.”

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it. I owe him more than one. Gave me a pocket Housman for Danny, foxed, wartime. No margins. They’d only erase them. Has a deaf old greyhound named Bishop Berkeley. Brought him to the Blessing of the Animals to annoy Fr. Osei. Osei finished his limerick for him. Asked me if the Housman had gone. Says when you leave something, look at it. Newman did. Threw a dinner at the cliff end of Del Playa. Told a man asking Yusuf about Fort Hood that Yusuf’s a guest, not a spokesman. Read our margins out loud. Stopped in the middle of Lena’s, and folded it away. Told Caleb he doesn’t answer devotion. Collected our margins. Read Lena’s on mine: Neither do I. The final’s oral, December 16th — each of us defends the other’s best argument, and he’s the opponent. Told the room to keep Yusuf’s chair. The last seminar: Lena said nothing for an hour, and he told us to note the date. By Friday we each email him which of the other’s arguments we’ll defend. If we pick a weak one, he’ll know. Both picks came in. Not surprised, not disappointed — at his age the same thing as joy. Wednesday, two o’clock. Come as you are. The oral: she’d sent him Augustine. Lena first, then me. He knew which one I’d picked. I don’t yet know what I know, he said. He said it was an argument; he’s told they still occur. Marks posted on the solstice. I did well, which he’d like me to understand is not the same as being right. He and Berkeley are spending Christmas in Marisol. Spring: PHIL 109H, The Novel as Moral Argument, Mondays and Thursdays at one in Hollis 302. Opposite ends of the table, for the safety of the others. He got the baby in the king cake. ‘For the first quarter of an hour you were civil, and I didn’t care for it. I find I care for this even less.’ Carthage is not on the syllabus. The Conversion of St. Paul: he did Saul for Caleb. He’s in New York Thursday, being rude to a churchman on a stage, so Greene moved to his house Wednesday with the State of the Union on — phones in the dog’s bowl, bring a guest, sides assigned: me for Sarah’s silence, Lena against. Opposite ends of a door. He turned the President off before the rebuttal. On the deck he asked where a Catholic goes at eight on a Wednesday. Give him my regards. He blessed my dog.

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday, behind the screen: love wills the good of the other — and that’s why it’s dangerous. Gaudete: rejoice is a command. Wednesday, behind the screen: I’m not avoiding the occasion, I’m scheduling it. Distance is a mercy; use it. Blessed us both for the road on the Newman steps. Come back. The first day back I gave him Father Dom’s message: we’ll see. He laughed. I told him I went at home. The night of the earthquake he asked the bishop if he could spare an old doctor. The bishop couldn’t spare a young priest. His friend Yaw from medical school is in Port-au-Prince — alive, operating in a parking lot. Saturday at three-thirty the light was on. Sunday he read Cana. Yaw has a generator now. Sunday at the 11:30 I didn’t go up. At the door I introduced him to Skye. He said her name. Then he said Wednesday, eight o’clock. Wednesday at eight the light was on, and he waited. Not gentle this time. I told him I think she’s the answer, and he asked: to what question? I didn’t have it. He said on Monday it was she who kept my Sunday, not me. The absolution isn’t a curtain between Fridays. He said Ma asked me the right question. He asked what will be different when I leave. Absolved me anyway. Penance: the Sower, slowly — the thorns. Then: go home tonight.
