body: “For your penance,” Osei says, “today’s Gospel. The Sower. You were not at the twelve-ten; I read it to the usual people and Mrs. Fitch.” “Read it tonight, slowly. Stay with the thorns, the part about what chokes it. The seed is strong. The ground is crowded.”

He says the Act of Contrition. It goes as it has gone since he was seven, as far as the last line, *and to avoid the near occasion of sin*, and there he slows down and says each word, because Osei isn’t going to hurry him and the father on the inside of the door is still running.
Behind the linen the shadow of a hand comes up. Osei says all of it this time, every word, in the voice that belongs to the altar and to nothing else.

“God, the Father of mercies, through the death and resurrection of his Son has reconciled the world to himself and sent the Holy Spirit among us for the forgiveness of sins; through the ministry of the Church may God give you pardon and peace, and I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”
“Amen.”
“The Lord has freed you from your sins. Go in peace.”
“Thanks be to God.”
“Jack.” Beads, and a breath.

body.text: “You asked me to tell you what to do, and I said no. This is small, and it is not a penance, so you may refuse it.”
body.else: “This is not a penance, so you may refuse it.”

body: “Go home tonight. To your own bed.”
“Yes, Father,” Jack says, not sure yet what he has agreed to.

He comes out of the closet with his knees stiff from the kneeler. In the nave two red cups are lit at the Marian shrine, a long way down the aisle, and the whole church smells of lemon oil and wax and the end of a day.

Mrs. Fitch has gone, and her lamp with her. On the card table, under the plastic wrap, a single lemon bar waits on a napkin with a Post-it on it in her hand: *Mr. Costigan — for the walk.* He takes it.

On the front steps the A-frame is black at his back and the moon stands high over the Channel, nearly full, and Ocean Road is empty both ways: Delgado up the hill to the left, Del Playa down the hill to the right. The RAZR is in his pocket, off since the dog’s bowl. He doesn’t turn it on.

choices.key: After confession Father Osei told you to go home. You went home.
response: He turns up the hill, with the Sower going in his head without its words yet. He will need the book.

choices.key: After confession Father Osei told you to go home. You went to Del Playa.
response: He turns down the hill. He tells himself he is going to tell her where he has been, and that is true, and it isn’t why.

s16h.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:05 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE CURB — THE SAAB, TOP DOWN
body: Halfway up the hill from Ocean Road he sees the Saab. It’s double-parked in front of Delgado with its top down, in January, the hazards blinking orange along the row of parked cars, and a boy from the second floor with a laundry basket on his hip gives it a wide berth on his way in. Skye is behind the wheel with the blanket off Sol’s porch around her shoulders and the moon up over the eucalyptus behind her. She has turned in her seat to watch the hill instead of the dorm door, so she sees him the whole way up.

He comes around into the street on her side and puts his forearms on the top of her door. Up close she smells like the porch she came from: popcorn, and somebody’s chimney down the lane, and the cold.
“Okay,” she says. “Hale. I want the heckles. All of them, word for word, don’t clean them up, because I’ll be able to —” She breaks off.

She looks at him in the orange of the hazards, at whatever has come up the hill on his face from the cliff end of Del Playa, and she lets Hale go. She gets up on her knees on the seat instead, takes the blanket off her own shoulders, and puts it around his, over the Carhartt, and tucks the end into his collar like a bib, and sits back down in her sweater.
“Did you go?” she says.
“Yes.”
“So Sunday you go up.”
He nods. She nods back, as if they’ve shaken on it.
“I read the part about the screen,” she says. “Twice. I had notes. I’m saving them for when you’re not tired.”
“Okay. The bit.” She wraps both hands around the top of the wheel and sets her chin on them. “I’ve been holding it since seven. It’s getting heavy.”
“Go.”

“You remember the couple.” Her chin comes up off her hands and one hand goes flat over her heart, and she’s the wounded one, from Sacramento, forty winters cold in his own house. “Last week he finally won. Five to four. He got his hands on the thermostat, and he’s being *very* gracious about it.” Down into the collar of her sweater, ancient and bow-tied, one finger raised: “*It was sixty-eight for a reason.*” She comes back up. “He wrote a dissent about it as long as a phone book. He read some of it out loud, in front of the whole street.”

“And tonight the man from across the street comes over.” She does the President with no words at all — the chin, the pauses, a hand that cuts the air into reasonable pieces — and at the end of it he turns, slow, toward the front row, where the couple sits in their robes being told in front of the neighborhood that they’ve left the front door open and anybody at all can walk in.

“And the new neighbor.” She folds her arms inside the sweater and sinks in the seat until she’s a man in the front row, and shakes her head, small and steady, side to side, while her mouth shapes *not true* with no sound behind it. “Moved in four years ago,” she says, out of the side of her mouth, still shaking it. “He isn’t even in the couple. He just lives next door and disagrees through the window.”
Jack is laughing, has been since the thermostat — helpless, hanging off her door with his head down on his arms.

“And *Tomás*.” Both her hands go up over the windshield, high, holding nothing. “On the porch. With the sign. LIAR. And he hasn’t decided. He points it at the President. He points it at the neighbor. He points it at the couple, both of them, for the thermostat. The man from Virginia comes on and he points it at him on principle before he’s said a word, and Sol is filming every bit of it, so he turns it around on Sol, and Sol just keeps —”
“I love you,” Jack says.

It comes out of the laugh the way a step comes out of a run. He didn’t decide it. He’s hanging off her door with his head half down on his arms and Sol’s blanket around him, still laughing at a man with a cardboard sign, and it’s out, in the street, in the orange of the hazards, and he hears it after it’s gone. Nobody on Glenwood Avenue says it out loud; they say *text me when you get there*. It’s true anyway. He knows it by the time it’s out — knew it, maybe, before that, at whatever red light she was sitting at when she said Nonna’s prayer for the first time.
She stops with her hands still up, holding the sign that isn’t there.

The street has gone very wide and very quiet. Somewhere on the fourth floor a stereo stops between songs. Her hands come down, slowly, and take the wheel at ten and two, in a car that isn’t going anywhere.

“No,” she says. “No — wait. That was —” She looks at him as if he has walked onto her set in the middle of a take. “That was *mine*. I had it. I’ve been holding it since seven, I *told* you it was getting heavy — the bit was the run-up, Jack, Tomás was the button, I was going to land it on Sol and turn around and —” She reaches for a voice to finish it in. Cassidy comes, sweet for half a line, and goes thin. “— there was a whole —”

And then she sees his face, and stops talking. He’s smiling at her. Wide, from one side of his face to the other, in the middle of the street, with his arms on her door and nothing he could do about it if he tried.

And then when you sat up and told me the good doesn’t get cancelled, and that time it was right there, and I put it back again, because then it would have come out as a *thank-you*.” Her hands are still at ten and two. “I was going to do it properly. I was going to do it *first*.” She lets go of the wheel. “I love you.”

s16ha.music: Ray LaMontagne — “You Are the Best Thing”
body: She’s the one who turns the iPod on, after — reaching past him to the dash with her other hand still caught in the front of the Carhartt — whatever comes up, and she doesn’t skip it. It comes out of the door speakers so low it’s mostly piano, under his elbows.
“I’ve said that on a soundstage forty times,” she says.
He waits.

“To a man with a microphone taped to his chest.” She looks up at him over the top of the windshield. “I counted, in a makeup trailer. Different men. Same tape. They put a mark on the floor so the light gets your eyes when you say it. And it’s always the girl first, Jack. They write it that way. The girl says it, and the man gets the reaction shot.” She shakes her head at the street. “Nobody ever got there ahead of me. Not on a page, not off one. Not till about ten minutes ago. And mine didn’t have a mark. That’s the first one that was mine.”
“What did they do after? The men.”
“Went to their trailers.” She takes her hand out of his jacket to fix the blanket where it slid. “One of them asked me to sign a headshot for his niece. With the tape still on.”
He has nothing clever for that, and doesn’t go looking for anything.
She sniffs, once, and sits up straight behind the wheel. “Okay,” she says. “Now Hale. Word for word. I was promised.”

So he gives her Hale, as close as he can get it: the freeze in January, *somebody on his staff has been reading Dante*; and the glass pointed down the chamber at the half sitting on its hands, *the only people in that room doing what they actually think*, and then at the half on its feet, *the only people in it who will get anything done*.
“Again,” she says. “Slower.” He does it slower, and her lips move along with his, stealing it. Then they stop. “He’s wrong about the sitting ones.”
“He’s Hale. He’s wrong for a living.”
“Sitting isn’t thinking. I’ve worked on sets where half the crew sits on its hands. That’s not conviction. That’s a union rule.”

“In Youngstown,” Jack says, “the ones who sit now stood up for every one of those speeches first. Carter. Reagan. Every one of them. The mills went anyway.” He hears his father in it and lets it stand. “My dad sits. He earned it.”
She thinks about that with her chin on the wheel. “So sitting’s what you do after standing didn’t work.”
“Yeah.”
“Then it isn’t conviction either,” Skye says. “It’s grief with good posture.”
He opens his mouth to answer that and finds he hasn’t got one, and she watches him find out, and looks extremely pleased with herself in the orange of the hazards.

He kisses her over the door. It’s slow, with the engine idling under it and her fingers hooked in the open front of the Carhartt to keep him where he is, and the cold coming up off the steel into his forearms, and Sol’s blanket sliding off one of his shoulders and her catching it one-handed. When it’s over she doesn’t start another. She sits back in her seat with her hands in her lap and looks at him, and laughs at herself, and wipes her eyes with the heel of one hand.
“Go up,” she says. “You have class in the morning.”
“Your blanket.”
“It’s Sol’s. Sol has a closet of them.” She puts the car in gear herself. “Keep it. You look like the third shepherd from the left.”

She pulls out from beside the parked cars with the hazards still going, remembers them halfway down the block, and kills them. At the corner, under the streetlight, her arm comes up out of the open top, straight up, and she holds it there the length of the turn.

He stands on the curb in Sol’s blanket. Delgado goes up over him, lit in rows. On the fourth floor, in his own window, the blind has been pulled a little way out from the frame, and when he looks up it lets go.

s16p.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:10 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, THE PORCH — THE SWING
body: Del Playa after nine on a Wednesday is half party and half library: a beer-pong table on a front lawn under a work light, a girl on the porch three doors up with a highlighter and her boyfriend’s head in her lap, bikes locked to every railing on the block. Sol’s porch light is on. Through the screen door the speeches are over and the panel of experts has the television, and Tomás is arguing with every one of them.
Skye is on the swing in Sol’s blanket, going a little, one foot on the boards. She sees him at the gate. The foot comes down and stops the swing.
“You came straight here.”

It comes across the porch like a fact she’s checking — ten past nine; St. Brendan’s at the top of the hill; she can count — and her face is glad and suspicious of it at the same time. “Is that allowed?”
He doesn’t explain it. He comes up the steps and sits down on the other half of the swing, and the driftwood takes his weight with a creak from both hooks and swings back.

She looks at him in the porch light. She puts her hand on his chest, inside the open Carhartt, on the flannel over his breastbone, and keeps it there long enough to feel him breathe twice. She takes it back under the blanket.
“Did you go?”
“Yes.”
“So Sunday you go up.” She tells the street so, and pushes off with her heel.
“I read about the screen,” she says. “I have follow-up questions. Later. They’re good ones.”

The screen door opens a foot. Sol looks out, sees who it is, hangs a second blanket over the back of the swing behind his head. Through the gap Tomás is telling a man in a red tie that he has never set foot in Ohio.
“Okay,” Skye says. “The speech. Sit there. Don’t help.”

She gets up with Sol’s blanket around her like robes and goes to the light switch beside the screen door. “This is the thermostat.” One hand on her heart — Sacramento, wounded, cold in his own house for as long as anybody on the street can remember — and the other on the switch. “*Mine.* After forty years. Five to four.” She flicks the porch light off and on again, just to feel it work. “And I want everyone on this street to know I’m being *gracious*.” And she folds down into somebody very small and very old in a bow tie, and from somewhere around her collarbone, quavering and certain: “*Sixty-eight. Since Ford.*”

She walks the length of the porch to the far rail and turns, and the rail is a podium. No words. A finger that comes down on each reasonable point; the pause before the next one; the chin. The President turns from it to the front row and tells the couple, with all of Del Playa listening, that they’ve left the door wide open and anyone can wander in.

Now she’s down on the top step with her knees together, the front row, arms folded inside the blanket, looking up at the rail where the President was. She shakes her head. Small, steady, side to side, while her lips shape *not true* with nothing behind it. “Moved in four years ago,” she tells Jack out of the corner of her mouth. “He isn’t even *in* the couple.”

And she’s up again, and Tomás’s actual sign is leaning against the rail where he left it — shirt cardboard, LIAR in black marker, a paint stirrer taped on for a handle — and she has it over her head. She turns it on the rail. On the top step. On the light switch, both of them. On the screen door, where the real Tomás is still going at the experts. On the moon.
Jack is laughing so hard the swing is going by itself.
“He hasn’t *decided*,” she says, swinging the sign around. “That’s the beauty. He keeps deciding. Sol has the camera on him, so he turns it on Sol, and Sol doesn’t even look up, she just —”
“I love you,” Jack says, from the swing.

He’s laughing when it gets out. It comes up out of the laugh with nothing in front of it, and he hears it on the porch after it has already landed. In his family nobody says it out loud; they say *text me when you get there*. It’s true anyway. He knows it by the time it’s out — has known it, maybe, since a girl with a highlighter sat up on a Sunday night learning the word for what he owes, so she could keep his Sunday for him.
The sign stops, pointed at nothing, out over the steps.
The swing comes back under him and slows. Through the screen door Tomás is telling an expert where he can put his panel, and then, as if something has come through the wall, he isn’t.

“That’s —” The sign comes down to her side. “No. That was *mine*. I had *pages*, Jack — I mean I had it, I’ve been carrying it around since Monday, it was going to go at the end, after Tomás, there was a whole — I was going to say it *first* —” She hunts for a voice to put it back into, and every one she tries comes out the wrong size.

Then she sees his face, and quits. He’s smiling at her — wide, so wide it pulls at the corners of his mouth — sitting on a swing on Del Playa in two blankets, and he couldn’t have stopped it for money.

The first time it would have sounded like a *term*. The second time you’d just told me the good counts, and it would have sounded like *thank you*.” She straightens up from the rail, three feet away under the porch light. “I love you.”

s16pa.music: Ray LaMontagne — “You Are the Best Thing”
body: Inside, Tomás has run out of experts and turned the panel off. A record starts in the front room, low, and somebody turns it lower.

They end up back on the swing, Jack in the middle of it and Skye sideways with her back against the chain at her end. She puts her feet in his lap, reaches the porch post with her toes, and pushes. The swing goes out over the boards. She keeps it going like that, one push every time it comes back to the post.
“I’ve said that on a soundstage forty times,” she says.
“Forty.”

“To a man with a microphone taped to his chest.” Her toes find the post. “You hold still while his sound guy fixes it, and you say it, and they say cut, and he goes to lunch. They always write it for the girl first. The man gets the reaction shot.” Out over the boards, and back. “Nobody ever beat me to it before. Not on a set, not off one. And that was the first one of mine that wasn’t a line.”
He takes her ankle, where it’s cold, and leans across her knees to kiss her, and she meets him halfway, short and sweet, and then puts him back in his corner of the swing with both feet.

body.text: “You came from church,” she says. “In the dark.” She looks up at the porch light over them. “Monday you told me your priest wants me in the daylight. That’s a porch light, Jack. It’s on a timer. It doesn’t count.” The swing comes back to the post, and she pushes. “I’m not going to be the reason you can’t go up Sunday.”

body: So he tells her about Mrs. Fitch instead: the bulletin and the one lamp, the lemon bar he had to eat, and the Hail Mary she says every night now for the both of them, because her granddaughter showed her their picture on the computer.
Skye stops the swing with her toes. “Which picture?”
“She didn’t say.”
She pulls the blanket up over her face. “Oh, *God*.” And then, from in there: “Is that a sin? Saying that? About her?”
“Depends what you meant by it.”
“I meant *oh God*.” She comes up out of the blanket. “Tell her thank you. I’ll take all of them.”

They sit there with the swing going and the record going under it, and she makes him do Hale, finally — the Dante line, the half of the room on its hands — and makes him do it again, slower, so she can steal it. Then she argues with it. Standing’s cheap, she says; she has sat in studio audiences, and a man holds up a card that says APPLAUSE. He tells her about Youngstown standing up for every speech since Carter, and the mills going anyway, and his father sitting now. She pushes off the post with her toes and thinks about it out over the boards and back. “So the ones sitting are the ones who stopped believing the card,” she says, and he looks for the hole in it all the way out and all the way back, and doesn’t find one. When the record runs out it’s eleven, and the lawn with the beer-pong table has got louder, and he has class in the morning. He lifts her feet off his lap and sets them down on the warm place where he was.
He’s through the gate and two houses up the lane when she calls after him, loud enough for the beer-pong lawn.
“Jack!”
He turns around in the middle of Del Playa. She’s up on her knees on the swing with one hand on the chain and the porch light behind her.
“That was *one!*” she yells. “Thirty-nine to go!”

body.text: He did go to his own bed, eventually. First he sat in the east stairwell with the window up its six inches and Sol’s blanket around him, saying the Act of Contrition through once more, slowly, the end of it slowest, while the moon went over, until Priya came through on rounds at a quarter to twelve and told him the stairwell was not a chapel, and also not a campsite.
body.else: He walked back up from Del Playa after eleven with Tomás’s record still in his head, past the turn for St. Brendan’s, knowing the whole way up the hill which bed he had been told to go to and which porch he had gone to first.

body: Theo is asleep, or doing it well. He started the bottle’s story over again from his pillow when Jack came in — the ambassador, the widowed sister in San Marino, and now a dog at the vineyard who could tell a good year by the cork — and somewhere in the middle of the dog he stopped. The Rioja stands on Jack’s desk with not much left in it and the price sticker turned to the wall. Hollis is in his teacup on the nightstand.
Jack sits on his bed in the dark and turns the RAZR on for the first time since Hale’s dog bowl. It takes its time about it.

body: Nothing comes back. He holds the phone until the screen dims on its own, and then he gets up, quietly, because of Theo, and takes the Bible down off the shelf over his desk and sits back down with it open to Mark.

The penance was the Sower, slowly, so he reads it slowly. The seed on the path, where the birds get it. The seed on the rock, coming up fast with no root under it and burning off when the sun gets high. The seed in among the thorns, where the worries of the world and the pull of money and the wanting of other things grow up alongside it and choke it off; he goes through that part with his finger under the line, like Rosie. And the good ground, thirty and sixty and a hundredfold.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record. She wanted to know if the nun was real. Now they’re Facebook friends, and Lena signs her wall posts like letters. Gina found the boyfriend in about four minutes. Didn’t tell Nonna. Ashley Vrabel is going to Halloween as a prisoner. Orange jumpsuit. A tribute, she says. Lena read it once and gave me a line for her. Halloween: went as a nun, obviously. Ashley wore the jumpsuit. Gina said it — visit, not dress up as — and Kelsey laughed at Ashley for once. Ashley says she’s dead Monday. Ashley sat next to her in religion and didn’t say anything. Kelsey either. The radio says they’re firing the GM. Dad laughed, Ma says. First time since June. Tuesday she said the thing about Ashley Vrabel’s father in religion. Detention. She thought it would feel good. She heard Dad’s truck hit the can Monday night. Team Edward. Jacob is literally a dog. Monday she found Nonna at the bottom of the stairs, and called the ambulance, and went for Dad. Said sorry to Ashley. Told me in the next text. On the floor in Denver I asked her to look up a girl. She screamed. She’s sworn. ‘Not even the nun?’ Thanksgiving: met me at the door — on TV, in person. Took Danny’s call and said nothing. Printed the dock picture on Ma’s ink. Translated Nonna for Theo, mostly. Checked Facebook for me — Becca took it down. ‘You looked like you were doing a shift.’ Gave Ashley Vrabel the peace at the first candle. Still sworn. Christmas: kept it thirty days. Lifted a hand to Ashley Vrabel at the Orange Julius first, and Ashley lifted one back. Gave me the second season of *Sweetwater*, for research — and Rosie handed it to me in front of everybody. She meant upstairs. Put season two in the DVD player the day after Christmas, for research, and the whole family watched. Wrote Danny about the boat. It’s a yacht. Filmed everybody’s resolutions on Theo’s Flip. Found the baptism album before I did. “Who’s the guy?” At the door, in my ear: “Don’t let Ma find out from Facebook.” Tuesday: six thousand views; Ashley Vrabel showed the whole bus. Nonna lit a candle and won’t say for who. On my wall: FINALLY — the sister who knew first. Monday she found me on a celebrity blog before I did, and knew Danny’s jacket. A man from Mahoning County called Danny a name in the comments; she reported him, answered him, and called him one back — a Catholic one. She’s making Danny a card for Candlemas. Tuesday Ashley Vrabel showed her the picture in chem. Capitals. Wednesday, at three in the morning her time: Nonna wants a baptism name, for the rosary.
